subtopic: MEETING WITH WESTERN FARM LIAISON COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Your Honour is correct in saying that you have heard some references to this matter in this house during the course of the present session. It is true that questions have been put by hon. members to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture with regard to the possibility of such a meeting. Your Honour will recall that the replies given to those questions were always of an indefinite character, and indicated no definite arrangement in so far as the declared policy of the government is concerned.
It cannot be argued that there is any other procedure open to us in order to urge the government to arrange a meeting with the farmers of western Canada, because the agriculture estimates have been disposed of. It is true that while those estimates were before the house I took advantage of the opportunity to raise this matter, but the replies of the Minister of Agriculture were of the same order as the replies given to the members of this house by the Prime Minister to questions put on the orders of the day. The matter cannot be dealt

with on the next supply motion, because a supply motion dealing with agriculture has already been disposed of this session. This matter, therefore, that is now well over a year and a half old and that has not been finally dealt with, surely should be discussed in this house at this time, particularly when we are about to prorogue.
Your Honour will recall that this matter arose a year ago last May, when a delegation of some 1,000 farmers from western Canada came to see the government concerning a solution which they proposed for the distressed agricultural situation. The government, after carefully listening to the representations that were made by those farmers, said the matter would receive careful consideration. We were told, indeed, by the Prime Minister several days before the conclusion of the last session of parliament that the matter was still engaging the attention of the government, and that before the session terminated we would receive a definite indication of government policy.

think there are three grounds upon which the propriety of the motion can be questioned. The first two relate to the matter of urgency, that is to say whether it is of that urgency which entitles it to be moved at this time as a matter requiring immediate debate.
In that connection I should like to point out the first of the two grounds on which I suggest it is not urgent, namely that it could be discussed on a supply motion. I understand that there have been some discussions with regard to the final supply motion that remains to be introduced. I also understand that it was indicated that that motion would be called on Monday if desired. That being the case, if my hon. friend wished we could discuss this matter on Monday on a supply motion.
In that connection I will just refer Your Honour to page 90 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, where paragraph 4 reads as follows:
(4) A motion to adjourn the house under standing order 26, for the purpose of discussing "the serious situation in which farmers of Manitoba are at the present time, on account of lack of feed for cattle and seed grain and no satisfactory result can be obtained from the government for relief", was ruled out of order, because the subject matter thereof could be discussed either on the motion for the house to go into committee of supply or on a certain bill then on the order paper-
The second of those grounds does not apply here, but the first does apply.
This matter could also be discussed on a motion for the house to go into committee of supply, which I understand will be coming up on Monday. If hon. members wish it to be discussed then, they could indicate that they wish to change the plans for dealing with the supply motion and this matter could be discussed on Monday. Therefore I submit that the urgency of debate is not of sufficient measure to warrant setting aside the present day's appointed business to debate this matter, since it could be debated on Monday.
Second, on this question of urgency, I would like to stress what Your Honour has already pointed out, namely that the matter has been discussed on a number of occasions during this session. There was opportunity for discussion on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and nothing has been said yet, I submit, which indicates that it has acquired that sufficient extra degree of urgency since it was last discussed which would warrant an interruption of the business appointed for this day. So on those two grounds I submit that the motion does not meet the requirements of urgency of debate which is a prerequisite for the allowing of the motion.
The third ground is one which I raise with some reservations, but I think it should be put


forward although in my submission the first two grounds are adequate. The third ground is the question of whether the matter raised by this motion in the form in which it has been presented is within the administrative responsibility of the government. As I recall the motion it simply said "to discuss the urgent matter of the desirability of meeting with the members of the farm liaison committee". It makes no suggestion as to what action within its administrative responsibility the government should take. It seems to me that in order to meet this requirement of the rules it should make some recommendation or suggestion or criticism with respect to what the government should do as a matter of administrative responsibility within one or other of the departments that are empowered to deal with farm problems. I raise as a very real question whether the mere arranging of a meeting with a group which is not of a governmental nature and which is not made up of members of the government or of any government can be said to fall within the administrative responsibility of the government in the sense in which those words are used in paragraph 100 on page 89 of Beauchesne's fourth edition.
For those three grounds, but as I say primarily on the first two grounds relating to urgency, I submit that this motion is not in order at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, the urgency mentioned in the rule has nothing to do with the matter before us. Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, citation 100 (3), reads:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.

It calls for the interruption of the business of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance.
The matter proposed is the necessity of an early meeting between the government and the western farm organizations' liaison committee. It was because of the indefiniteness of that proposal that I perhaps asked for more argument than would be warranted, because I was not clear on what the hon. member wished the house to debate. It is obviously not the fact of a meeting, because that has no
Inquiries of the Ministry significance in itself. It is a meeting with respect to farm policy, I assume, that would give this motion any urgency.
In fairness to the hon. member I have tried to see some change in the relationship of the farm organizations toward this house and the government, and it is the government in this case that is referred to, which would warrant our taking the matter up again as a matter of urgency of debate.
Regard must be had to the substantial amount of time that has been spent in dealing with farm policy in the course of this session, whether it be deficiency payments or any other item of farm policy which might be discussed at the meeting which hon. members wish to urge on the government. Whatever the policy for discussion, it is a broad problem which, like the unemployment problem, cannot be the subject of a motion of this kind, in my view, unless there is some specific change, happening or event which has arisen since the general discussion in the house. There have been ample discussions in the house on farm policy, and I assume there will be further discussion in the house.
On those grounds which have been put forward and debated, I think, very fully, it seems to me the rule is not satisfied.

Mr. Speaker, on June 22 the hon. member for Vancouver East asked me the following question:
Can the Prime Minister make any comment on the report that the Vancouver city council has requested him to convene immediately a conference of federal, provincial, municipal, employer and union leaders to consider the present serious unemployment situation in British Columbia?


To which question I replied as follows:
I will examine the record to see whether or not representations have been made, and then give the hon. gentleman a reply.
As a matter of fact he was two days ahead. It was not until June 24 that a message to that effect was received by me in the late afternoon. So far as the answer is concerned to the several matters arising in consequence of this representation by the city council of Vancouver, the Minister of Labour will make the reply.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister received a request from the Vancouver city council to call a conference on unemployment in British Columbia. Certainly the advice and suggestions of provincial, municipal and labour leaders is always welcomed in the matter of finding jobs for Canadians and in maintaining employment.
Provincial authorities particularly are in an advantageous position, as they are more familiar with the situation in a particular province and possibly are aware of developing circumstances in that province which may alter or improve the situation. In this instance I might point out that at least one province has acknowledged its responsibility in this matter; that is the province of Quebec.
The federal government called a conference in July, 1958 dealing with the question of seasonal unemployment. That conference was attended by provincial, municipal and industrial representatives, including those of labour. As a result the federal government put into effect a municipal winter works plan which was responsible last winter for stimulating needed municipal works in the amount of $75 million, and in two winters provided more than 90,000 jobs on site.
At the present time the causes leading to manpower surplus in an expanding economy are under investigation in the other place, and the services of an outstanding economist have been engaged. Dr. Deutsch and his staff will continue to amass information during the recess in order that the committee of the other place may carry on its deliberations in the light of all the facts. Certainly the situation in each province will come under careful scrutiny. A number of organizations will be asked to submit information and suggestions to this committee, and some of them certainly will be from British Columbia.
In the Department of Labour studies are being carried on dealing with the effects of automation in industry. That department's research branch is keeping a close watch on the manpower situation across Canada.

Certainly the government is in close touch with what is going on, and such policies as may be invoked to deal with the situation will be announced at the proper time. Meanwhile all suggestions are welcomed, from whatever quarter they may come.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the hope of expediting the work of this committee, as in previous years I shall attempt to summarize for the committee the highlights of the fishery and the work of the department for the year 195960, the fiscal year just ended. I know you will realize that in order to achieve brevity I must leave out much of importance to particular areas; also, I shall be obliged to make generalized statements which may not always apply in particular cases.
First, I think the committee should recall the extraordinary hazards faced by our fishermen and the tragic loss of life experienced in so many families in the Northumberland strait area of New Brunswick last June. Earlier in the year there was the loss in Newfoundland of the trawler Blue Wave with all its crew. This spring severe storms off Nova Scotia have added to the toll. This list is not complete, but it brings home the hardships associated with reaping the harvests of the sea.
From a production point of view, 1959 was generally a good year, although of course not all areas showed increases over 1958. For the Atlantic region, dominated by the groundfish and lobster fisheries, the total value of the landings was the highest ever recorded. The preliminary total of $59.1 million was 16 per cent over 1958 and a 10 per cent increase over the five-year average of 1955-59.
The Newfoundland inshore fishermen who experienced a very short catch in 1958 enjoyed an exceptionally good year in 1959 in almost all areas. The draggers operating in the gulf and the deep sea vessels fishing out of ports in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland also had a very successful season. On the other hand the small line fishing boats had a poor year, particularly along the Gaspe coast and elsewhere in the gulf of St. Lawrence.
The situation as to markets for the products of the groundfish fishery was somewhat unusual last year. It was the salted fish branch of the industry which experienced a strong demand, while the frozen fish trade was less buoyant. Salted fish production was

substantially higher than in 1958, but a low stock position at the beginning of the marketing year, together with-

I wonder whether the minister would mind my interrupting and just suggesting to him that if he came forward and sat opposite the other microphone he would be a good deal easier to hear. He is between two microphones.
I thank the hon. member very much for his suggestion, and I will adopt it.
We really want to hear this minister.

When I was interrupted I was saying that salt fish production was substantially higher than in 1958, but that the low stock position at the beginning of the marketing year, together with some relaxation of trade restrictions in important markets, resulted in higher prices for the increased supply.
In the case of frozen fish, on the other hand, the relatively strong market of 1958 encouraged increased production and pressure of supplies on the United States market, with the result that inventories increased and prices declined. However, the situation has eased somewhat in recent months and the long term prospects are considered good.
The lobster fishery, only slightly less important than the groundfish fishery to the Atlantic coast, was late in starting in 1959 but was generally productive throughout the summer and fall, and on the average prices were somewhat higher than in 1958. In spite of heavy gear losses and a slight decline in price, the winter and spring seasons have been the best for many years.
The fisheries of British Columbia failed to repeat the record year of 1958. This was anticipated, as 1958 had included the high cycle year for sockeye salmon on the Fraser river. As a result the total pack of canned salmon was slightly less than 1.1 million cases as compared with 1.9 million cases in the 1958 season.
The market for frozen as well as canned products of the salmon fishery remained strong throughout the year, and prices were high. A productive season has been forecast for the 1959 winter herring fishery in British Columbia, and from a start in early October until the Christmas layover catches were running well ahead of those for the same period the year before. The rapid expansion of fish meal production, particularly in Peru, resulted in a sharp decline in world prices for this product. This problem with its serious effect on herring and whaling operations is of
Supply-Fisheries
major concern to and study by this department as well as by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
In 1959 the catch in the halibut fishery was a little higher than that of the preceding year, although prices were slightly lower. As the result of this development the total value of landings in British Columbia declined from $52.5 million in 1958 to $35.4 million in 1959. However, the 1959 figure was only slightly below the five-year average of $36.7 million.
Looking to the future, I think we may be confident that the long term prospects for the salmon and halibut fisheries are bright. There are problems in these fisheries, particularly with respect to production costs and conservation measures, but the market demand for a limited or gradually expanding production should continue strong.
Discussion of the Canadian fresh water fisheries in general terms is especially difficult because of the vast extent of the region included, stretching from Great Slave lake to the St. Lawrence. Within this territory over 600 lakes are fished commercially. In some areas there are distinct summer and winter fisheries, but for the region as a whole these tend to merge one into the other.
In the spring of 1959 an unusually late break-up delayed the start of the summer fishery in most areas until the middle of June. Catches thereafter were reported to be better than average everywhere except in Ontario, where a fall in the catch of pickerel and in the price of perch reduced the total value of landings quite seriously as compared with previous years.
Winter fishing operations got under way toward the end of November, and results were generally satisfactory. A declining trend in fishing intensity on Great Slave lake, evident for several years past, continued. It is attributed to the difficulty of recruiting crews for the arduous work of winter fishing and to other factors tending to raise production costs. On the other hand, for the first time an experimental winter fishery with trawl gear for smelts was conducted on lake Erie. In general, with rising prices at the turn of the year the outlook for the fresh water fisheries in 1959-60 improved, and total returns to fishermen close to the annual average of approximately $13 million were indicated.
The success or failure of the fisheries in a particular year is, of course, the result of a wide range of factors. Many of these factors are beyond the control of the fisherman. The role of the various services of the department is generally speaking to maintain and where possible expand the resource, and to encourage fishermen to take the greatest possible advantage of the opportunities available to

Supply-Fisheries
them. In the field of conservation and improvement of the productive capacity of the fisheries we cannot guarantee increased runs every year. Indeed, it is necessary in some instances to restrict the catch today for the benefit of tomorrow.
In the maritimes our chief worry is the lobster fishery. We continue to be confronted with the activity of the small minority who refuse to accept the necessity of regulation, but I am glad to say that it would seem that more and more the fishermen engaged in the lobster industry are realizing that the regulations under which they must operate are based on sound conservation principles and that it is to their own benefit to observe them. Co-operation in this regard has always been high, and I am glad to say that the exceptions are, I believe, becoming less and less. In any case we are continuing our efforts toward achieving complete support for sound conservation of this most important branch of the industry.
The department's information service is continuing its educational program among the lobster fishermen in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. Well attended meetings have been held in a number of fishing communities, with special speakers and films. Radio is also being used in this program.
In British Columbia, as I have indicated, the year 1959 was one in which the low cycle for most species of salmon occurred. Under strict management practices, however, escapement to the spawning areas was generally good. We were particularly encouraged by the apparent building up of certain runs of fall fish.
Fish culture, designed to overcome the effect of advancing civilization and industrialization, is one of the important phases of conservation. The year 1959 was important in this respect.
In the maritimes the transfer of 10,000 barrels of disease-resistant oysters from Prince Edward Island to stricken areas of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia was completed. To date the results have been good. The transplants have shown only normal mortality, and normal mortality is 7 per cent or 8 per cent or less. These oysters have grown well and have spawned, and it looks as if they will be a continuing race in this new environment in which they have been placed. We were also fortunate in having a year of very heavy oyster spatting, in Prince Edward Island especially. Our collectors produced over 600 barrels of small oysters, and this represents a tremendous amount of seed oysters which will be used to the greatest benefit of the industry when they become available for distribution.
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1
We continue to be pressed with problems from hydroelectric power developments, yet it is good to be able to report solutions in most cases. In Newfoundland, for example, the transfer of Atlantic salmon continued successfully from Little Rattling brook, blocked by a power dam, to Great Rattling brook. We are opening up the exploits system with new fishways, and we are continuing to check other developments and clear rivers of manmade and natural obstructions.
In the fisheries in the western part of the country the problems are manifold. We can, however, report success in the fishway at the Whitehorse dam in the Yukon, the removal of the rock slide on the Skeena river, and new fishways at Indian Falls. A study at Meziadin Falls on the Naas river has indicated how a natural obstruction may be overcome. Meanwhile the many fishways already installed continue to function well. Gradually the rivers are being opened up to more efficient migration.
During the year we had the opportunity, with more experienced staff, to turn our attention to other methods and wider applications. Construction of a 2,500 foot controlled flow spawning channel at Robertson creek, Vancouver island, gives us a chance to increase salmon spawning efficiency. Associated with this is a test flume which will be used by the department to test water intake fish deflector devices and by the fisheries research board to continue long term studies on salmon behaviour. Experimental rearing ponds have also been built to study problems of this nature associated with multiple water use projects. In addition we are developing a lake spawning beach.
A major item in the 1959-60 estimates covered the acquisition of a new large patrol vessel to replace the M. V. Cygnus which has operated in the maritime area for several years. The new Cygnus was commissioned late last year. The estimates before you contain a substantial item to provide for a similar vessel to be delivered in 1962 which will operate in Newfoundland waters.
The fisheries research board continued its nation-wide research activities throughout the year. This organization is being pressed more and more for information on fundamental problems and answers to current practical questions. The first full year's operations of the board's deep sea research vessel, the A. T. Cameron, fully demonstrated the value of this vessel as a tool for biological and oceanographic studies on the Atlantic banks and adjacent waters. One of its important cruises covered Davis strait and Baffin bay and into Canada's Arctic waters. Much of the work of the A. T. Cameron, as

well as that carried out at the biological stations at St. John's, Newfoundland and St. Andrews, New Brunswick, has been directed to the groundfish investigations required by the international commission for the northwest Atlantic fisheries.
On the Pacific coast a major effort is being put into salmon and herring studies by the board's station at Nanaimo, in response to recommendations by the internatonal north Pacific fisheries commission. Among other activities in this area was an extensive tagging and recovery program on pink salmon migrating through Johnstone strait, carried out in co-operation with the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission and workers from the state of Washington.
A new and important field of investigation by the board was a "blitz" survey of the fish resources of the larger lakes of the barren grounds in the districts of Mackenzie and Keewatin. This investigation was carried out by teams of researchers operating under the direction of the board's Arctic unit operating out of Montreal.
To complete this hasty sweep of the board's activities from coast to coast, I should also mention its activities in the great lakes region. Here the board is acting as the Canadian agent of the international great lakes fishery commission in carrying out experiments on lamprey control under contract from that commission. The board has also initiated biological studies of the fisheries of lake Superior.
Another highlight in the expansion of the board's facilities for research was the opening of the new technological laboratory on the campus of the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. These improved facilities will undoubtedly enable the board to make an even greater contribution in this phase of its activities to all branches of the industry.
Significant progress has been made during the past year in the field of fisheries industrial development. Important achievements in this connection have resulted from the increasing degree of co-operation among the department, the provincial administrations, the fishing industry itself and many private industrial concerns, seeking a potential outlet for their products in the modernizing of the fishing industry. The recent addition of industrial engineers and fishing gear specialists to the department's industrial development service has added greatly to the advice and assistance that can be made available to the industry right across the country.
The department's fish processing experimental plant at Valleyfield, Newfoundland,
Supply-Fisheries
has been directing its main effort to problems associated with the salt fish industry, and has succeeded in developing a new salt fish product which shows promise. Samples have been sent to many parts of the world, and the first reactions are most favourable. New fish splitting machinery has been acquired and modified to meet specific Canadian requirements, and new techniques for curing, handling and drying fish have been developed in order to improve the product and reduce processing and handling costs.
The introduction and demonstration of new fish catching equipment and methods to areas where they were previously unknown is having significant and advantageous effects on fishing operations in many parts of Canada. The short term hiring of fishermen who are highly specialized in the use of specific types of fishing gear has been introduced with considerable success, with a view to accelerating the introduction and demonstration of catching equipment in areas where it has not been in use.
Work on the design and development of improved types of fishing craft is going forward at an encouraging pace and the first vessel, featuring a multi-purpose function, has been built in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia and already launched.
In the field of inspection the highlight of the year was the "Canada Inspected" program which began on April 1, 1959. Under this program any plant processing fresh or frozen fish can be granted continuous inspection of its products by departmental officers, provided that the plant meets rigid requirements in respect of construction, equipment, sanitation and operation. Similarly, comprehensive standards were developed for the product. All frozen fish meeting these standards, which have to do with freshness, workmanship and freedom from defects, may be marked with a maple leaf design containing the words "Canada Inspected", while fresh fish may bear a similar design containing the words "Processed under government supervision". I might say that the products which bear these labels have a considerable advantage as far as the marketing of fish products is concerned, because it increases very considerably their acceptability to the consumer of food products.
By the end of February, 1960 a total of over 30 plants had been approved under this program. Limited advertising on the part of the department has met with very good consumer response.
In order to ensure that the fish processing industry benefits from the latest advances in quality control, new equipment and the findings of biological and technological research,

Supply-Fisheries
the department convened courses lor fish plant foremen at Halifax and St. John's, with courses being planned for other centres.
During the year the inspection service also assumed inspection responsibilities in the province of Quebec, and a new administrative area was established to discharge these responsibilities. Most of the personnel involved were taken into the federal civil service from the former inspection service of the province of Quebec, and I must say it speaks very highly for their qualifications to say that the transfer was carried out with a minimum of difficulty and delay.
Despite difficulties in recruiting qualified home economists there was a considerable increase in the amount of television and radio work by the consumer service during the year, as well as the regular demonstrations that are carried on by these specialists for women's groups, schools, institutions, restaurant associations and so forth. The consumer service together with the information and education service issued a new fish cook book which has won critical acclaim from food editors as well as from house wives. The first run consisted of 10,000 copies in English and 3,000 in French. The book sells for $1. The first issue has been completely sold out and a second run is now on order with the Queen's printer. The rerun will consist of 10,000 copies in English and 5,000 in French. The department is continuing its general consumer advertising and will also enter into a limited campaign in grocery magazines with particular emphasis on the availability of government inspected products, which is an excellent selling point.
The economics service continues to study economic problems that are brought before the department affecting the Canadian fishing industry and fish trade. In recent years, for example, many difficult problems of management have arisen in the salmon and halibut fisheries of the Pacific coast. In response to requests from representatives of fishermen and fish buyers the economics service has carried out an intensive investigation into these problems. Field work of the investigation, under the charge of a consultant from the University of Manitoba, was completed some time ago. In preparation for an investigation into the lobster fishery of the Atlantic coast, where a similar management problem exists, the economics service in 1958-59 carried out a survey of all primary fishing enterprises in the maritime provinces to obtain background data for a detailed study of such questions as the interdependence of lobster-ing and other fishing operations, of lobster-ing and farming, etc. The study will be initiated in this current fiscal year.

The economic service has concerned itself with the improvement of statistical services and the solution of problems of industrial development or modernization. A number of projects in these fields are still in hand, and among the reports released in 1959 was one on costs and earnings in assisted fishing enterprises and one on production costs in mechanized fish curing operations.	The
major current project, however, is a study of the economy of the Canadian fresh water fisheries production and distribution.
As I indicated in my opening remarks, the market situation throughout 1959	was
generally satisfactory; but I said also in my opening remarks, of course, that this is a generalization. There are exceptions. In only a few cases were we requested to investigate the possible use of price support legislation, and in no case was such action necessary.
The rebate of 50 per cent on the cost of salt to fishermen was continued and is again continuing in the estimates before you. The program of building 20 community stages in Newfoundland, initiated as a constructive income supplement following the catch failure of 1958, has now been largely completed by the Department of Public Works. At the same time the bait service carried on by the department in Newfoundland has been expanded and its efficiency improved. The vessel insurance plan continues to grow and provides more and more protection to small boat owners. At the end of March of this year more than 5,400 vessels valued at over $16 million were covered under this plan.
In the course of these remarks I have had occasion to mention several of the seven international fisheries commissions on which Canada is represented. Members of the committee are familiar with them, so there is no need of my outlining them now. The results to date show clearly that international cooperation and co-ordination in the field of fisheries conservation are a prime requisite to offset the deleterious effects of increasing range and efficiency of fishing fleets. As time goes on and world population increases it is inevitable that the fishing pressure on the living resources of the sea and of inland waters will increase proportionately or even at a greater rate.
While the estimates before the committee today, of course, are confined to those of the Department of Fisheries, I might point out in passing that there are activities carried on by a number of other departments of government which directly affect the fishing industry. I will not attempt to list them all, of course. I should like to acknowledge that the department does service a great deal of useful assistance from other department of government.

A major contribution is made to the fishing industry by the Department of Public Works in the construction of wharves, dredging, harbour development, breakwaters, and so forth. Similarly, the marine service of the Department of Transport is of vital significance to the fishing industry. As another example, the Department of Finance administers the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Department of Labour, of course, administers unemployment insurance as it applies to fishermen and also co-operates in technical training programs in co-operation with provincial governments. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources also co-operates with us fully, especially in questions of water resources and Arctic development generally as far as the fishing industry is concerned. The very heavy dependence of our industry on export trade brings us in close contact with the Department of Trade and Commerce, particularly the trade commissioner service, and there are many others; but I will not bore the committee by listing them further as they are not directly concerned with these estimates. I think, Mr. Chairman, I probably would be out of order in discussing them, strictly speaking, but I wanted to make this explanation because these are matters that are frequently brought up on the fisheries estimates by hon. members of the committee.
Members of the committee will note that there is a slight reduction in the estimates of the department of this year, a reduction of $1,393,277, to be exact. This has been achieved without any reduction of essential services. This may sound contradictory on its face, but that is not so. The reduction has been achieved chiefly by three sets of circumstances. There have been instances where increased efficiency has been achieved and correspondingly a saving in money. There are other instances where relatively new programs have been developed recently, and this year it has been possible more accurately to forecast costs in regard to them owing to the experience that has been gained over the last couple of years. Then, perhaps I mill not say the largest but one of the largest items of saving is this. Several large construction programs have been nearing completion, and the annual costs in some of them have been greatly reduced as a result.
On the other side of the balance sheet, of course, there are increases in expenditures such as increases in wages, especially with regard to crews on vessels, and the annual automatic increases in pay of civil service employees, and so forth.
I am sorry to have taken up so much of the time of the committee, but I feel that
Supply-Fisheries
perhaps a general review of this sort may form a basis on which orderly discussion can take place. I shall be pleased to try to answer as accurately and as concisely as I can any questions hon. members may have, and I will listen with great interest to any suggestions hon. members may make as to ways in which benefit can be created for the fishing industry of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by thanking the minister for his very comprehensive review of his department and of conditions that obtained in the fishing industry during the past year. In particular I should like to thank him for the human touch in his reference to the hazards which fishermen have to contend with, as was exemplified by the disaster in the Northumberland strait and by the loss of the Blue Wave which, incidentally, touched my own riding very much because the entire crew of that vessel was from the riding which I represent.
I do not suppose there is any department of government which is of such great interest to the Atlantic region as that under the minister's administration; and particularly, of course, to my own province which, perhaps more than any other province, is dependent upon the resources in our coastal waters. The references which the minister made to the work of the research vessel A. T. Cameron, to the biological laboratory at St. John's, Newfoundland, to the work being done at Valley-field and the problems which are being overcome in connection with the successful transfer of salmon up river systems are all of intense interest to my own province.
I am only going to take time to deal with three or four points mentioned by the minister. He ended his remarks by stating that there had been a slight reduction in the estimates but that this would not result in any reduction of essential services. I say at once that I know of no one who has any complaints to offer about the minister's department and the way it is administered. I think we are all very happy with the work the minister is doing, the capability of his staff and the intense interest and sympathetic co-operation which I am sure everybody experiences with regard to problems they put before the department.
However, perhaps I might correct the minister's figures slightly. He said that the estimates were down by $1,393,000, but the situation is not quite that bad; because I think he left out the figures in the supplementary estimates. When they are taken into account we find that the actual estimates for this year total $20,344,090, which is a little less than $1 million below the figure of $21,332,867 for last year.

Supply-Fisheries
But, Mr. Chairman, I must express my own disappointment that this reduction has taken place, because on examining the estimates I see that the bulk of the reduction has been made in two very important items. There has been a decrease of $604,180 in the industrial development item and a reduction of $107,160 in the Newfoundland bait service item.
In his closing remarks the minister referred to the completion of the community stage program and I gathered from what he said that 20 stages have now been completed.
No, the program is not really complete. There still are three, I believe, to be completed.

What concerned me was that when the minister spoke his words seemed to indicate that when these 20 stages were completed that would be the end of the community stage program. I sincerely hope this is not going to be the case, because I think the community stage program is one of the best innovations that have been brought into existence since the minister took office. It is certainly a very beneficial program and one that I feel should be not only continued but expanded. In Newfoundland it is of special importance in the efforts we are making to concentrate the fishermen in larger settlements and to get them to use joint facilities instead of each person having his own stage, thereby establishing conditions under which a better quality product can be produced.
There is still another reason why the community stage program should be continued. It affords the fishermen of my province a safeguard against price control. The fresh fish plants do not always compete as to price for the fisherman's product, and the existence of a community stage affords him protection in that he always has the choice of selling his fish fresh or selling it salted. This has two results. It ensures that the fresh fish price will not go below what the fisherman might realize if he salted his fish, and it also provides another safeguard in that very often when the school is at its peak and the catches are extremely large, the fresh fish plants cannot handle all the fish and unless the fishermen had facilities for salting they would be obliged to sell their fish for meal.
The minister's remarks today indicate that the prospects for meal prices going up in the future are not very good. We all know what has happened since Peru entered the market, and we know the effects on our herring industry and on the whaling industry. I think it would be a serious hardship to many of

our Newfoundland fishermen if they could not salt the excess catch which the plants are not able to absorb. I hope the minister will reconsider any idea he may have of discontinuing this program.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock I had reached the point where I was urging the minister to reconsider the continuation of the community stage program. I had pointed out that it is very essential to the welfare of the fishermen of my province that this program should not only be continued but should be expanded. The community stage program has so much merit that I think it should not be confined to the province of Newfoundland but should be a general program which would embrace any part of Canada that was in a position to take advantage of it.
In urging the minister to continue the program I will say that I think there is room for improvement in the policy which governed the program which is about to be completed. I do not know what the position is at the moment, but I do know that last year there was a time when we had three different kinds of programs in connection with community stages. There was one which was provincially inspired and financed. There was one which was totally federal, to which the fishermen made no contribution at all. Then there was another one which was financed partly by the federal government and partly by the donation of labour by the fishermen themselves. I feel from these three different programs it should be possible to develop one single program to be made applicable to all of Canada.
I drew the minister's attention to the fact that the industrial development vote had been reduced by $604,000 from last year. While we appreciate the necessity of paring expenses and doing everything to balance the budget, it could be false economy when that saving is achieved at the expense of the development of our resources. I do hope that next year we will see this industrial development item not only restored to its former size but greatly expanded to take in all phases of a larger program of industrial development for the fishing industry.
I was very much interested in the minister's remarks concerning the pressure on our fisheries which is resulting from the intensification of fishing and by an increase in

the number of countries that are sending fishing fleets to our fishing grounds and particularly to the Grand Banks. There was a time when the fisheries of the Grand Banks were held to be inexhaustible. I do not believe any thinking person could hold that view any longer. Certainly it is most urgent that steps be taken before too late to make sure that our fisheries resources are not depleted. I realize that provisions governing areas outside of territorial waters require international agreement, and international agreements are not easy to come by; I realize also that international committees are working on this problem but progress seems to be very slow and unless results are speeded up it may well be that action will be taken too late.
It is my own opinion that the method of catching fish by draggers is a wasteful one and steps should be taken to find less wasteful methods to substitute for it. The draggers which tow these huge nets along the bottom of the ocean destroy a tremendous amount of young fish which are killed in the process of being hauled to the surface, just as small children are very often killed and trampled on in a mob. The pressure created by the tremendous weight of fish over them when the fish are being hauled in destroys a lot of young fish which are not of commercial size. Some fall out of the net before they get into the boat, while others that are taken into the boat are thrown overboard because they have no commercial value. I believe if agreement could be worked out under which all the nations would agree to use a different method of fishing, perhaps even going back to the hook and line method, as much fish as should be caught under the circumstances would be caught. Certainly this method would prevent large numbers of fish from being destroyed and wasted.
This problem of conservation is closely related to the limits of our territorial waters. I think it was a tragedy when the United Nations law of the sea conference at Geneva failed to reach agreement on this problem by a single vote. At the present time there is nothing but chaos. There is no accepted law of the sea either as to the extent of territorial waters or as to the extent of the coastal waters which any country can claim as a preserve and monopoly of its own fishing fleet. I think we have now reached the point where it is possible for Canada and the United States to reach an agreement as far as the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards are concerned and work out a joint agreement fixing the limit of 12 miles for our own territorial waters. If agreement cannot be reached, then I think Canada would be well justified in taking unilateral action and proclaiming her own limit
Supply-Fisheries
which would extend the control of the fisheries to 12 miles offshore.
These problems of conservation of our fisheries and the extension of our territorial waters are related also to our patrol service. I am glad to learn from the minister that a new boat has been built to replace the old Cygnus and that these estimates contain provision for a new boat for the patrolling of Newfoundland waters. But if we are going to have an effective patrol service we need many more boats than we have at the present time.
Most of my fishermen are complaining-and this is the situation not only on the south coast which I represent but on the northeast coast as well-that at night huge concentrations of foreign trawlers are gathered together in such great numbers that they look like a floating city. We must have a sufficient number of boats to be able to patrol these areas at all times. You cannot rush one small boat, however fast she is, from one spot to another spot three or four hundred miles away. There is need for at least three boats on our coasts in order to do an efficient patrol service on our coastal waters.
This encroachment on our inshore fishing grounds is proving to be a tremendous handicap and a hardship to our own inshore fishermen. The fishery on the east coast of Newfoundland this year is very poor and some fishermen think that one of the reasons is that these grounds have been dragged over by foreign draggers. I hope the minister next year will be able to provide for at least two more patrol boats in increased estimates. If we had more of these patrol boats they could also be used as rescue boats in the winter time for the coastal service and for those ships that are engaged in the winter fishery.
The other matter to which I wish to refer is the bait service. I have already noted that this year there is a decrease of $107,000 in that item. I realize how difficult it is to administer the bait service. I realize all the problems that are connected with it and I realize that the problems are made perhaps more difficult by the fact that this particular service is confined to the province of Newfoundland as part of the terms of union. However, I think it is possible for the federal government to work out a bait program which could be applicable to other provinces as well. I do not understand what the need of this service is on the Pacific coast. However, there must be communities on the Atlantic coast which could benefit from a similar service although from personal experience, I know that the need is not so great as it is in Newfoundland.
This year I think we are providing for five units. From a rough calculation which I have

Supply-Fisheries
made I would think there is at present a need for about 50 of these small portable bait units which have proved to be so successful during the past few years. But if we supply these units at the rate of only five a year it means that it is going to take ten years at least before the needs of the fishermen are supplied; and by that time some of the earlier ones will need replacement. I believe that the time has come when we can perhaps take another look at our bait service policies and can work out something a little bit different from what we have at the present time.
I should like to see worked out an arrangement whereby the fishermen themselves would be able to own and control these small portable bait units. When I say that I am thinking not only of fishermen in my own province but of fishermen in other provinces as well. I understand that these units cost about $6,000 at the rate at which they are supplied, which is about ten or 12 a year. Fifty of these units would cost about $300,000. If they were purchased in quantity or were manufactured in quantity the price perhaps would be considerably less than that. But taking the total value at, say, $300,000, I think that would supply all the bait requirements we have at the present time in Newfoundland.
The provincial government of Newfoundland has a fund which it is holding in trust for the fishermen. If the federal government were prepared to make an offer of providing these units at half price it might be possible to work out an agreement whereby the provincial government would place at the disposal of the Newfoundland fisheries federation some of this money which could be put out on loan to fisheries locals and small co-operative groups of fishermen who would be able to purchase their own units and repay over a period of perhaps ten years. It would not be a very big sum if they had to pay say $3,000 over a period of five years or ten years. They would then have the benefit of being able to administer the small units themselves and to work out whatever particular scheme is most suitable to the conditions under which they are obliged to operate.
I would think, though, that the federal government also should supply technicians to train the operators to look after these units and also perhaps maintenance men to keep them in order. If that could be done then the federal government's role would be mainly the maintenance of central depots from which the smaller depots could be supplied and I think that would be a proper federal responsibility. In addition, of course,

there would also need to be some bait carriers for the purpose of carrying the bait from the central depot to the smaller ones.
This is only a brief outline of an idea which I have had. I think it is feasible and I also think that where there is a will, there is a way. If everybody concerned would put the interests of the fishermen first, it should be possible to work out a system which would remove a great many of the disadvantages and difficulties with which the federal department is now obliged to contend and which would at the same time improve the service to the fishermen.
I was disappointed on one count in the minister's presentation this morning.
