I am sure we all listened with a great deal of interest to the resume of the minister on the operations of his department during this past year, and also his views on the state of the fishing industry at the present time. I want to say that I was most disappointed at the brevity of the remarks of the minister regarding the state of the industry in British Columbia, particularly the herring industry and the whaling industry. As the minister knows-as a matter of fact he commented on it-the British Columbia whaling industry is perhaps the most recent casualty of the fishing industry.
I have noted that the fisheries association of British Columbia, in putting forward the reasons why there is no whaling industry in British Columbia, point out three factors. They are (a) the whales which are available off the British Columbia coast are much thinner than those found in other whaling areas, and consequently the unit yield per whale is lower; (b) they state that the distance of British Columbia from principal market areas creates a substantial freight cost as a handicap; and (c>
the fisheries association stated that the level of all production costs was high in British Columbia compared with competing sources of whale products, namely Japan, Russia, Norway, Holland and Great Britain.
I would point out that these conditions are outlined by the fisheries association of British Columbia have always obtained and they most certainly have obtained in the past ten years when the British Columbia Packers Limited have been persisting in their endeavours to operate a continuous annual whaling industry.
So it is with a great deal of regret that circumstances have brought about the situation where there is no whaling industry in British Columbia this year, and that is having an impact on British Columbia. Because it

must be recognized that the whaling operation now closed means a loss, I understand, of approximately $600,000 annually in wages and hundreds of thousands of dollars lost to such supply and service industries as petroleum companies, the shipyards, rope works, vessel outfitters and so on. So this is a serious matter to the fishing industry of British Columbia and I had hoped that the minister would have had more to say other than just to comment upon the fact that these industries had closed, that it was of serious concern to his department and that studies were being made of the situation.
Hand in hand with the closure of the whaling industry in British Columbia we have the closing of the herring industry which affects a great many more people than does the whaling industry. As was mentioned by the minister, there was a very good catch in the ten weeks preceding Christmas when I understand there was a record catch of some 166,000 tons. Yet around Christmastime there was a closure of that industry and according to the newspapers it is being continued this year. The fishing companies in British Columbia point out that one of the reasons why they have had to shut down operation is the fact that in 1958 the price for herring meal was $2.70 a unit and nine cents a pound for herring oil, but now these prices have declined to $1.48 a unit for herring meal and six and one half cents a pound for herring oil.
They also point out that there are other reasons which have brought about this situation, and one is the appearance of large new producers in South Africa, Angola and, above all Peru. We have heard a great deal about the entrance of Peru into the herring market. There is a unique point here of which I think some mention should be made, and it is that at the same time the fisheries association of British Columbia have put a closure on herring on account of the low prices for meal and oil, and because they say they cannot stand the competition from Peru, the largest of the fishing associations of British Columbia, out of its profits made along the coast of British Columbia, has established itself in Peru and is using its past and present profits from British Columbia to build up this industry in Peru, as I say supplied by British Columbia capital, about which condition the associations of British Columbia complain and maintain they cannot meet. I think that is not only a paradoxical situation but one which requires some very considerable attention.
I also note, that the fisheries companies in British Columbia point out that one reason for the closing of the herring and whaling industries fishing off the Pacific coast is the competition they are now facing from edible
Supply-Fisheries
oils. They state that the Canadian industry has encountered severe competition in the Canadian market because of the greatly increased production of animal and vegetable oils, and they name soybean, sunflower and rapeseed.
This brings up another question. It is a serious one and I believe one upon which we should have some comment from the minister. The whaling and herring industries are shut down in British Columbia because they cannot meet the increased competition in Canada of the edible oils which are available at lower prices for the manufacture of shortening and of margarine. Yet it is a fact that the very producers who have brought about this situation are those which are subsidized by the federal government. I know that last year we had the subsidy to the soybean growers. Last week we had an announcement from the Minister of Agriculture that the subsidy to the soybean growers is going to be continued in the next 12 months. So we have that peculiar situation of a lowering of prices and where the herring meal or whaling meal or the marine oils can no longer compete because the price has been forced down by subsidized agriculture in Canada.
We know that help has to be given to agriculture, but we have the situation, which I think all should note, that a government subsidy on the one hand has killed an industry on the other. That gives an idea of the sort of thinking and planning which has to be applied to our economy. I think I should point out that if certain phases of agriculture get into difficulties the government and parliament come through with subsidies. If the railroads are in difficulties we come through with subsidies. If coal mining is in difficulties we help them. But if fishing in British Columbia is in difficulties and certain phases of it are being closed down there is no help whatsoever. At least I do not know of any except that the matter is of serious concern to the government and a deep study is being made of it.
I think that is rank discrimination. Financial help is given to industries of varying kinds across Canada yet we have not seen any action taken to help those two important phases of the fishing industry in British Columbia which are not just in difficult times but are completely shut down, affecting, I believe, some 225 to 250 employees in the whaling industry and I believe between 1,200 and 1,500 in the herring industry.
I admit it is not enough to raise these matters and point out what I am sure is already known to the minister, the impact this is having on the fishing industry in general

Supply-Fisheries
and the economy of British Columbia in particular. I feel that under this item we are entitled to have from the minister more than a comment to the effect that the situation exists, is of deep concern to him and his department and studies are going on. We are entitled to know what type of study is being conducted and what approach the departmental officials are taking to this serious problem.
I was interested in reading that South Africa also feeling the impact of Peruvian competition sent a delegation to Peru to see if it were possible to work out a marketing, pricing and production agreement. I presume they were not successful but at least an effort was made. Does the department have any such idea? Has the minister heard the results obtained by the South African delegation sent to Peru?
I was also interested in learning that the fishing industries of the United States, the United Kingdom and South Africa asked their governments to convene a meeting of all nations interested in fish meal protein to study the problems that have arisen. I am advised by the fisheries association of British Columbia that they asked the government of Canada to participate if such a conference were convened. Has the minister been in touch with other countries that have a concern similar to that of Canada to discuss the possibilities of there being convened a conference of the major countries concerned with fishing for the purpose of resolving existing problems? If no action has been taken yet will the government take the initiative in this respect? If the government cannot take the initiative in attempting to bring together representatives from the nations concerned conditions will get worse. The situation will worsen if corrective action is not speedily taken.
Before the item carries I sincerely hope the minister will take us more fully into his confidence with respect to the situation in the whaling and herring industries and concerning the studies now being carried on, and will tell us when he thinks it might be possible to make constructive, progressive and corrective announcements.
Will the minister also say something more about Canada's position regarding the 12-mile limit in relation to fishing. This is of keen interest to the maritime provinces and British Columbia. I believe it was the view of the government that it would have liked to see a general agreement on the 12-mile limit. The government was unsuccessful in presenting that view or in achieving a compromise at the meeting held in Geneva because of the lack of one vote.
I know that the fishermen and the fishing industry and unions on the west coast are

concerned about the question of territorial rights and authority in relation to offshore fishing. Would the minister speak about the Canadian position concerned the three, six or 12-mile limit? With respect to the three-mile limit will he explain if it is from headland to headland? That makes a great deal of difference on the coastline of British Columbia as the hon. gentleman knows.
I hope I have said enough to indicate the seriousness of the situation as outlined. I trust that the minister will give us some hope that in the near future the whaling and herring industry in British Columbia will resume operations.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with other hon. members in commending the minister on the excellent attention he has given to the fisheries in all parts of Canada. I should like to make a few observations and suggestions in the interest of the fisheries of the great lakes area. In doing so, I fully realize the fact that the Ontario provincial government has jurisdiction over these waters with the exception of international problems but I consider the restoration of suitable commercial fish to the lakes an international problem.
Our federal fisheries department is making a determined effort toward the betterment of fishing through the efforts' of the great lakes fishery commission in lamprey destruction; however, to date only lake Superior has received any attention in this respect. Lamprey are numerous in all the lakes. Therefore their destruction is a tremendous undertaking and scientists and others in charge of this work feel best results can be obtained by concentrating on a specific area for a certain time. Even providing the program works out to expectations there is not much hope of completely exterminating the lamprey and, furthermore, much time and money will be expended in the effort. However, I feel it is a worthy project but it seems to me that other angles should be considered and some action taken.
We know the lake trout have almost become extinct and the population of rough fish in the lakes has increased at a rapid rate. Most of these fish are maintained on the same food as that needed for trout production. Therefore I would recommend that necessary funds be made available for the removal of as many as possible of these fish from our lakes so that lake trout and other desirable fish are given the best possible opportunity to re-establish themselves when the lamprey menace is to some extent removed.
Such a program would provide a livelihood for quite a number of the idle fishermen,

and with the exception of Georgian bay could be institutd on a co-operative basis with the United States. A market could be established for certain varieties of these fish and I believe sufficiently large quantities of such fish are available to produce enough revenue to take care of at least one-third of the cost of the program.
When I spoke during the 1959 session in the interest of the great lakes fisheries I suggested the introduction of sockeye and spring salmon into these waters. This idea met with the approval of many people, especially the fishermen. However, according to press releases appearing at intervals since our scientists left the impression that such a program would not be feasible, but their reasoning was not too convincing.
In support of my suggestion I will take as an example our experience with the rainbow trout which were introduced into the great lakes from the Pacific coast. Their increase in numbers has not been phenomenal. However, a satisfactory steady growth in their population has justified the soundness of their introduction. This past spring rainbow trout were observed going up every suitable stream flowing into Georgian bay to spawn and in the largest numbers since their introduction into the great lakes.
They are now supplying our sportsmen with very good fishing. Some excellent catches have been made during the past few weeks, with individual fish weighing up to 12 pounds. The rainbow trout is not considered a commercial fish. However, they are making a worthy contribution to the rebuilding of tourism which at one time was attracted to our district by lake trout.
Worthy of mention is the fact that very few rainbow were carrying scars from lamprey attack. With this apparent resistance to lamprey, the rainbow trout provides a promising future for sportsmen and tourism.
To support my claim that Pacific salmon do hold some promise for commercial fishing in the great lakes, I relate the incident of the taking of three salmon at three different locations in lake Superior late last summer. The fishermen were unable to identify these fish but the fisheries research office of the Minnesota division of game and fish identified them as pink or humpback salmon and they were mature fish. It appeared a mystery for a time as to how these fish came to be in lake Superior. Some time later it was established that in 1956 a few small fish escaped from a hatchery at Fort William where they had been incubated from eggs from the west coast. The establishment of a salmon run in the rivers of Hudson bay was the purpose of this experiment. However, it now
Supply-Fisheries
appears that there was a greater survival from the few that escaped into lake Superior than from the 200,000 fingerlings that were planted in Goose creek, a tributary to Hudson bay, as there is no record of any survival there. Consequently it would be logical to presume that others of those escapees into lake Superior also survived and continue to thrive in the fresh waters.
This incident bears out the claims made by Tasmania fisheries and the department of fisheries of New Zealand that they successfully transplanted spring and sockeye salmon to their inland lakes and a satisfactory cycle has beeen achieved. Furthermore, the sockeye salmon which became isolated in British Columbia inland lakes have established themselves there and have continued to reproduce. I believe the coast salmon have an advantage over lake trout from the standpoint of survival, considering present day conditions in the great lakes. We have not only the lamprey menace but the smelt which many fishermen feel may be a greater enemy of our desirable fish than is the lamprey.
They are a small fish and much of their diet is very small fish and the spawn of larger fish. Consequently I would suggest that fish such as rainbow, sockeye and other coastal salmon that spawn in the headwaters of our streams would have a very decided advantage in respect of survival. The lake trout and splake which deposit their spawn on the shoals where the smelts and suckers are frequently swarming are constantly losing their reproduction to these predators.
Thus when one essential condition of environment has reached a limiting level which prevents a species from flourishing but still allows survival, a very minor deterioration in this condition will suddenly decimate the population. Conversely, a slight improvement in this condition of environment will be followed by an upsurge in population. Therefore the removal from the lake of as many of these predators as possible could influence a favourable balance for lake trout production.
Second, the introduction of a new species of fish, such as the sockeye or other suitable commercial salmon, which would spawn in the headwaters of our streams, could result in a successful production which would satisfy our needs should our efforts to re-establish lake trout or splake fail.
The introduction of splake, a cross between lake trout and speckled trout, into the Georgian bay has been given much publicity. According to figures released, almost 300,000 fingerlings have been planted in this area since 1956 with some apparent success. Evidence of any production could not be expected

Supply-Fisheries
so soon. However, splake weighing up to four pounds have been taken by the fishermen and their reproduction cycle can start at the third year.
Some fabulous claims have been made as to the possibilities of the splake but I am doubtful as to how long this crossbred fish can continue to reproduce its kind when it is placed in the environment of the lake trout. My thought is that more and more of the splake eggs will be fertilized by lake trout and that the production will soon revert to lake trout.
It seems to me that if we are to create the best possible conditions for the establishment of a splake population, or the re-establishment of a lake trout population, a closed season for at least two or three years should be imposed. Splake are being fished continually and in 1959, 11,000 pounds of lake trout were taken in lake Huron and Georgian bay. If we are ever to stock our lakes it is essential that these meagre remnants of the species must be retained as breeding stock.
Worthy of mention at this point in my remarks is the recent success of the Japanese fisheries in crossing Pacific salmon with trout from their inland lakes. Their scientists hope to mass produce this new fish in their lakes.
In conclusion, I would suggest that if we are to provide ideal conditions in our waters for fish propagation some immediate action should be taken to curb the constantly increasing pollution of our lakes by industry, shipping, lake bottom oil drilling and other harmful sewage.

Mr. Chairman, first I should like to say how much I enjoyed listening to the minister's report on the activities of himself and his department. Second, I should like to say that I looked forward to hearing him and I moved up to the front benches to make sure that I heard him and I stayed here to make sure that he would hear me.
As often as I can, as the committee knows, I talk about the fisheries of Newfoundland and in fact the fisheries of eastern Canada because I believe that the fisheries are growing in importance as our population increases and as the need for more work, for more industry, for more people grows, so grows the importance of our oldest industry.
If I may repeat something I have said before, no nation, no matter how many new industries it develops, can afford to neglect an old industry because in a properly expanding economy all industries are necessary if the nation is to be prosperous. But today, instead of launching out and talking about what we need and the extras that we want, I should like to pause briefly and talk about some of the things which have been accomplished.

For many years the fisheries in Newfoundland were conducted in the same way as they were shortly after John Cabot discovered Canada and returned to England with the story that the waters around the new found island were full of fish. For many years the fishery was conducted, using the same type of gear, the same type of boat, in other words the same type of equipment, with very few changes. That was not so bad during the years when progress was comparatively slow and when the industrial revolution had not been heard of; but when modern times came and practically every other industry became modernized, the lag in the development of the fisheries became very serious indeed.
During the first decade before Newfoundland entered confederation-and I am speaking just of Newfoundland now-changes began to take place. It was then that the fresh fish business began to grow. After we had entered confederation all of our economy got a very great boost and fishery development was speeded up. New fresh fish plants in addition to those already existing began to be built and older ones began to be enlarged. It was recognized at that time that the fisheries of Newfoundland needed several things. Production had to be increased and the method of curing had to be improved.
By and large over the years much improvement has occurred in the fishing industry. There is a much greater degree of industrialization today than there was 10 years ago. Artificial drying has reached a stage that we would have been very happy to have had ten years ago. At this point I should like to refer to the report of the Newfoundland fisheries development committee, known as the Walsh report, which was issued in 1953 and which makes excellent and informative reading even today. Only seven years ago it was stated in that report:
Along that coast development should, In the view of the committee, be by centralization of the salt fish industry at a number of plants located at suitable places in large areas of production in the inshore fishery and near grounds on which long-lining can be successfully carried on. The operations in these plants would be as fully mechanized as possible and the aim should be ultimately to produce light salted fish by mechanical drying.
That was seven years ago and I am very happy to say that since that time much improvement has been made and mechanical drying has to a marked degree-I was going to say to a large degree-supplanted the old expensive method of sun curing and the handling of the fish by the fisherman and his family for which they received very little. Their labour was practically free.

Production and the means of production have been improved as well. The establishment of experimental stations has been of tremendous value. I should like to comment in this regard that I think it is a pity that the public know so little about the great work being done quietly by the experimental and research stations. Their work probably is not of a type that commands headlines or is surrounded by glamour but it is very vital work and has a great and important bearing upon the future of the fisheries. Its importance will make itself felt in more dollars and cents in the pockets of the fishermen which after all is the purpose. The department can be proud of the work it is doing and I should like to see it intensified and broadened. These are some of the things which have been done; industrialization, mechanization and the development of the means of production.
Many of these things were incorporated in the report issued by the government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland in 1953. The program since then has been by and large a broad and beneficial one but I think that time shows up the weaknesses in any line of endeavour and is probably showing now where the gaps in the program are. Without pretending to be an expert on the matter, I should like to mention several gaps which seem to me to be obvious. First, I think more attention should be given to the Labrador fisheries. I believe that with industrialization is coming a greater demand for fish and this at a time when there are probably fewer fishermen than there were in 1953.
I have no figures for Nova Scotia but I have reason to believe that the fish plants of that province depend largely upon Newfoundland fish for their raw material. Industrialization has brought about a greater demand for fish and the result is that more and more attention is being focused on Labrador by people in the fishing industry. I should like to see the resumption of the Labrador fisheries, not necessarily the old floaters which, although they served a good purpose in their time, were not the most economical method of producing fish, but a Labrador fishery tailored to meet the needs of the times and designed to fill the need which is beginning to exist already and will certainly exist to a greater degree within the next few years.
Before the Labrador fishery can be improved as it should be something must be done to help those fishermen living on the Labrador coast already and who throughout the years after the floater fishery failed continued the fishery on the Labrador coast. It is their product which is more and more in demand. Like many other small businessmen 79951-0-350
Supply-Fisheries
regardless of their line of endeavour one of their great needs is capital. They may have all the knowledge in the world as to how to catch fish but unless they have proper boats and good gear they are not going to be able to catch the amount of fish they should. It is evident that the fishermen need better equipment in order that they may prosecute the fishery off the Labrador coast. Therefore I should like to ask the minister to keep in mind the need for some means by which fishermen can get small loans in order to replace and repair equipment, some means by which the federal government can assist the fishermen directly to replace fishing gear and property lost from time to time by storms. I believe that once this property is replaced, once they have the gear, they will be able to operate on their own, but they need help in order to get started. I would ask the government to look into that matter.
I would also ask the Minister of Fisheries to consider carefully the possibility of increasing the bounty on boats and broadening the whole scheme so that small fishing boats will come within the limits of the bounty and fishermen who wish to build small trap skiffs will be able to obtain some assistance from the government in the form of bounties on small boats.
The minister mentioned bait, and here there is another hole in the program which must be plugged. I am very glad to say that improvement in the bait service is already evident but nevertheless this is one instance where the improvements of today are still not sufficient. In most places along the Newfoundland coast there is a perennial shortage of bait and thousands and thousands of quintals of fish which should be caught and sold to the benefit of the fishermen and the people of Canada are left in the water because the fishermen have no bait. Therefore I would ask the minister to continue and enlarge the bait program.
Whereas bait depots are good things and holding plants to supplement the bait depot service are perhaps a better thing, I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, that small holding plants or freezing units should be available to the fishermen. I think these could perhaps be provided in connection with community stages better than in any other way but even where the fisherman has his own property a method should be found by which he will be able to buy freezers for his bait.
May I enlarge for a moment upon the bait situation. I should like to go back to what I mentioned before-this is something for the minister's research department-and that is the possibility of developing artificial bait.

Supply-Fisheries
I maintain that if as much attention were given to the development of artificial lures for codfish as there is to the development of lures for trout we might be able, to a large extent, to do without frozen bait. For instance, squid is undoubtedly the best form of bait that the fisherman finds. It is certainly not the shape of the bait which attracts the codfish because the squid are cut up in shapeless chunks and put on the hook. Then the fish go for it. I do not know whether it is the taste or the smell that attracts them. I was wondering if a liquid could be devised which tasted or smelled like squid-what I might call essence of squid-and put in drums. These drums could be shipped around to the fishermen who could bait their hooks with a piece of sponge or something like that soaked in this liquid which would carry all the aroma and taste of squid. Then the fishermen's bait problem might be solved. I should like the minister to ask his officials to look into the possibility of developing artificial bait in a form which could be shipped around in cans. Then instead of making one big jump ahead into frozen bait, we might make one big step back into the canning age and see if we cannot can this essence of squid.
I believe that if the program which has been followed for some time, were rounded out so that the small fisherman who operates independently with a small boat and with a limited amount of gear could be helped to get his boat and his gear into condition so that he could fish effectively, then we would have taken a long step forward.
I would refer the minister to the report of the Newfoundland fisheries development committee of 1953. I believe this report served an excellent purpose and was used as the basis of much that has been done. This is a good thing because so many reports, once they have been printed, seem to be put to one side and are forgotten. Then later another royal commission is appointed which produces another report. I would suggest that this report, which obviously has not been forgotten, be looked at again very carefully. It is eight years old and an effort might be made to bring it up to date. Certainly there must be some weaknesses in the forecasts. After all, the commission that made the report had to make it on the basis of the knowledge they had at that time. If the report were gone over carefully today it could be revised on important points and used as the basis for a more up to date and more complete program. I should like to see that done. Undoubtedly the minister has read the report, and I should like him to consider the possibility of having it revised. I am sure that if he does he will see that his

program, good as it is, can be enlarged and, in some cases, speeded up.
Canada produces only about 10 per cent of the world's production of salty codfish. I feel it is a shame that we who have the best fishing grounds in the world should be catching so little. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned territorial waters. I should like to endorse what he said. The waters around Canada are being exploited regularly by the ships of foreign nations. Not too long ago a whole mess of trouble was stirred up because a plane flew across the territory of another country. Foreign ships operate regularly off the coasts of Canada and when the minister mentioned he was having a new boat constructed I was tempted to suggest that she be so equipped that she can drive off these poachers.
In so far as community stages are concerned, I have said in this house before that the community stage program was a wise and enlightened one. I hope it is continued and I hope that it is extended so that some community stages will be built in Labrador. If I may refer to Labrador for a minute, I would say that more ships are fishing there now than heretofore. I believe it was sometime around 1840 when the fishermen from Conception and Trinity bays in Newfoundland began to fish the Labrador coast. They found the European fishermen were there ahead of them. We find they are still there today. There seems to be a tendency for the fish to move northward, and if that is so then we must depend more and more on Labrador for the fish to keep the fish plants of the Atlantic provinces in operation.
Not only do we want the Labrador fisherman equipped so that he can be an efficient fisherman, not only do we need community stages, but we badly need communications so that the fishermen can communicate with one another along the coast and with the rest of the world. Communications are essential to the proper development of the fisheries. I was very glad to hear the minister refer to the work being done at Rattling Brook and the Exploits river and the fish ladders there. I was pleased to note that such progress has been made and I hope it is continued because I do think there is a very great spawning ground there for salmon.
In conclusion, I should like to again stress the necessity for increasing salt fish production and fresh fish production. I do hope that the fishermen themselves will share more in the profits of the industry. The fresh fish business seems to be in a healthy condition and it is my hope that the fishermen will share in the profits of that industry. In so far as salt fish are concerned, we are going

to have that industry with us for a long time. Mankind has been using this stable product since time immemorial. I should like to see more salt fish plants in northern Newfoundland and Labrador. Certainly the cod fishery can be increased. It is pretty well known, I believe, that the fish are there and that more of them can be caught without jeopardizing a constant supply. One of the best ways in which we can assure that there is increased fish production in Canada is to see that the fishermen themselves are able to catch fish, have the means to catch it and the places in which to work once they have done so.
As to the minister and his department, may I say this, and of course any remarks I make are divorced from any, shall I say, political position which the minister may have. But in so far as he is the Queen's minister of fisheries and in his work as he guides the Department of Fisheries which is one of the most important departments in the government of Canada may I say: more power to your elbow.

I welcome this opportunity to speak briefly on the fisheries estimates that are before the committee at the present time. I should first like to commend the minister on the detailed report he has given of the work that has been undertaken by his department. I might say that it is a report which clearly indicates the concern of the government over the problems at present faced by fishermen. I was most interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador when he spoke of the need for perfecting an artificial lure. I might add that there is one available at present. It was perfected in Norway and it is called the Norwegian jig. It is approximately eight inches long, is shaped somewhat in the form of a spoon and is most effective when used in catching cod, haddock or any other groundfish.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question.
Certainly.

Will the hon. gentleman come up and join the rest of us near the centre of the chamber-as it is permissible to sit anywhere in committee-in order that we can hear him. We are interested in what he has to say.

I think I can speak loudly enough. I have a few notes here. I will speak a little bit more loudly so that hon. gentlemen can hear me.
During the Easter recess and at a recent special event in Nova Scotia I had an opportunity to speak to many of the fishermen
79951-0-350i
Supply-Fisheries
and also to the executives of fishing companies in my riding. These discussions brought a number of points forcefully to my attention and I should like to mention them for I believe they are worthy of consideration by the minister.
At the present time it would appear that the problem causing most concern among the fishermen on the east coast is the age of the existing ships in the deep-sea fishing fleet and the fact that these ships are not being replaced with modern up-to-date fishing trawlers. The average age of these wooden trawlers is approximately 12 years. Some of these trawlers are already obsolete when compared with new trawlers that are built by other nations. Accommodation for the captain and the crew falls far short of the comforts provided fishermen on new trawlers built by other countries. But aside from this point, there is among fishermen a growing fear that when the present ships are worn out or require expensive repairs in order to keep them operating they will be unemployed because of the lack of provision by the industry for the replacement of these existing ships. In the event this should happen we must ask the question: how important is the fishing industry to Canada?
The annual report of the Department of Fisheries for 1958-59 answers that question for it begins with this statement and I quote:
With an annual catch of all species of fish and shellfish amounting to nearly two billion pounds, worth about $116 million to approximately 80,000 men engaged in commercial fishing, Canada ranks as a leading producer and exporter of the world's fishery products.
To me that sounds like quite an important industry. The export value of the 1958 catch was $155 million, about two thirds of which came from the United States and most of the remainder from the United Kingdom, continental Europe and the Caribbean countries. In my opinion the fishing industry makes a great contribution to correct our imbalance in trade, especially with the United States-It is an industry that has for years stood: upon its own feet without too much assistance from government. But today it can no longer absorb the increased cost of production while selling its products in competition with state subsidized producers.
I was pleased to note in this year's estimates that continued assistance will be provided groups of fishermen desirous of constructing small draggers or long-liners up to 65 feet in length. However recent studies would indicate the assisted fleet at present accounts for about 20 per cent of the total groundfish landings on the east coast, with the company-owned deep-sea and the inshore boats providing the remaining 80 per cent.

Supply-Fisheries
This modernization program carried out by the fisheries deparment has contributed substantially to the replacement of small boats, and has provided greater opportunity, more security and a higher scale of living for the inshore fishermen. However, the industry as a whole depends on the larger trawlers and draggers for a constant supply of fish, and it is this type of ship, 100 feet in length or larger, that provides steady employment on shore in the fish plants and afloat for the fishermen, especially during the months from November through to April when the weather is inclement and the inshore boats cannot operate or operate only sporadically.
Ultimately therefore the burden of modernization, replacement and expansion will fall on the company-owned fleet of deep-sea fishing trawlers. Money for this replacement cannot be secured by raising prices, for two thirds of the industry's sales dollar-wise are to foreign markets, in competition with fishery products from nations with a lower cost structure. At the present time many of the materials and much of the equipment used by the industry are admitted either free of duty or at a low rate of duty, and within certain limits trawlers can be purchased outside this country. Perhaps this problem is of more direct interest to the shipyards than to the fishing industry.
However, most Canadian deep-sea fishing captains and their crews prefer wood to steel in a trawler or dragger 100 feet in length or even up to 125 feet in length. This is owing to the greater buoyancy of the wooden ship. Something needs to be done if our shipyards are to provide and be in a position to undertake even necessary refit work. Increased depreciation allowances to existing operators would encourage more venture capital in the industry and I would suggest that the government give serious consideration to this problem. It is a problem calling for bold, imaginative steps; and unless building costs of fishing trawlers in Canada can be reduced, or investment in this highly venturesome industry can be made more attractive, we will shortly have a fleet of obsolete ships incapable of providing steady employment or maintaining our position in world markets. For the benefit of the committeee, I might say that recently the President of the United States-it was on June 12-signed the fisheries assistance act of 1959. The bill provides: (1) a fishing vessel subsidy of up to one third the cost of construction, if built in a U.S. shipyard under approval of the department of defence.
I should like to point out there that what our friends to the south of us are doing

apparently is that they are co-operating through their defence and fisheries departments and are building ships that would be suitable in time of war.
The federal subsidy shall be $2.5 million per year for three years; eligible are those building vessels operated in a fishery for which escape clause relief had been recommended by the tariff commission but denied under the trade agreements assistance act and to certain fisheries found by the secretary of the interior to be injured by increased imports of fish or shellfish products.
I am not advocating that we take that type of action but I would point out the action which has been taken by the nation to the south.
In what other way can we help our fishermen? I believe we should give serious consideration to repealing the law which discriminates against our east coast fishermen who are competing with foreign vessels. At the present time we have a 12-mile limit, and other speakers this afternoon have mentioned this problem. This does not mean 12 miles of protected ocean for our Canadian fishermen; on the contrary it means nine miles of protected fishing rights for all other nations except Canada. Our fishermen using ships up to 65 feet in length can fish with all foreign fishermen up to three miles of our coast, but any Canadian fishermen in ships larger than 65 feet are unable to start fishing operations until they are 12 miles off shore.
This three-mile limit apparently came into general use around 1793 when it was adopted by the United States as the limit of its jurisdiction for neutrality purposes. During the nineteenth century many maritime states, inspired by British and United States practices, came to use the same limits, but it never won enough universal acceptance to become a rule of international law. In the absence of any uniform practice with respect to the width of territorial waters modern international law can be said to lay down no rule except that every state is entitled to claim at least three nautical miles.
After world war II the international law commission, organized under the auspices of the United Nations general assembly, selected in 1949 the question of the territorial sea as one of its topics for study and report. The commission's deliberations on this subject disclosed, however, that many of the difficulties encountered in 1930, when the question of territorial waters was discussed under the leagues of nations at The Hague, still presented major obstacles to any agreement. The claim to a 12-mile limit has met with such widespread opposition from other countries

that it will probably never be universally accepted, for we have seen this proposal again rejected this year at the conference called in April at Geneva.
A recent incident points out the absurdity of the present situation. The Canadian fishing trawler Sea Hawk was fishing in North bay near cape St. Lawrence in company with a fleet of some 15 or more Spanish and Portuguese trawlers. They were fishing approximately seven miles off the tip of Cape Breton and the operation of the draggers was so extensive in that area that the Canadian fisheries patrol boat Cygnus had to thread her way through this foreign fleet in order to get to the Canadian trawler and bring her to port, where the captain and owners were fined $50 and costs for fishing inside the 12-mile limit.
In my opinion there was no doubt a time when we were trying to build up a case for a 12-mile territorial coastal belt that this action made some sense. However, since the failure at the Geneva conference for the second time in two years to reach international agreement on the law of the sea there is no sound argument left for continuing this law and I would suggest that it be repealed. Canadian fishermen as taxpayers help provide wharves, harbour facilities and deep water channels for the convenience of foreign draggers and trawlers. In my opinion these Canadian fishermen are entitled to equal fishing rights with deep-sea fishermen from all other countries.
At the present time the most vigorously expanding shell fishery in the maritime provinces is that of the sea scallop. During the past year combined landings of scallop meats from Canadian and United States fishermen amounted to 23 million pounds. Of this total United States landings accounted for 18.7 million pounds and Canada produced 4.3 million pounds. Percentagewise the United States landings were up 25 per cent while the Canadian landings increased to 54 per cent over 1958. The increase in landings was the result of increased efforts by offshore boats fishing the Georges bank off the Maine coast and brought to the fishermen of the maritimes earnings in excess of $1,600,000.
At the request of the international commission for the northwest Atlantic fisheries joint experiments are being carried out with a large mesh scallop drag in an effort to find a way to reduce the numbers of small, unmarketable scallops which are damaged and wasted by handling on board fishing vessels. The government is to be commended for its action in this regard.
However at the present time there is very little knowledge available about the manner

in which scallops breed and multiply. I would suggest the fisheries department give consideration to studying this problem with special attention given to studying the early free swimming larval stages. This information is vitally important when endeavouring to determine the densities of future scallop populations, and this information would of course be most useful to the fishermen presently engaged in this industry.
There is some indication at the present time that the size of the scallops landed represent a particular year class. The current high production will no doubt deplete these stocks of older scallops and could result in a levelling off and lower production due to smaller scallops being landed in 1961 and 1962. Because of these facts and the economic importance of this industry I hope the fisheries department will give further study to the items I have mentioned.
I would like at this time to commend the minister and his staff for the gratifying progress that has been made in overcoming problems which for many years have beset the oyster industry in the maritime provinces and to mention in particular the results in curbing the epidemic which by the end of
1958	had ravaged almost all the main oyster beds in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The 3,200 barrels of disease resistant oysters from Prince Edward Island transplanted in
1959	and the balance of the program of transplanting 10,000 barrels this year will go a long way toward re-establishing this profitable and worth while inshore fishery. It is also gratifying to note that in all areas examined the transplanted oysters have suffered only normal mortality or less and continued good growth has been demonstrated.
At the present time the fishing industry is beset by many problems. During the past year the production of fresh and frozen ground-fish products, chiefly fillets and fish blocks, was considerably above that of the previous year. However, demand for these products had begun to weaken, resulting in a downward pressure on prices at both the primary and secondary stages of production. The deterioration of the Canadian fish trade position in the United States market, where some 85 per cent of the total production is sold, has been attributed to the increase in imports from Iceland and other European countries. At the same time there is evidence that total supplies have tended to exceed export requirements over the past ten or 15 years and this has acted as a continuous depressant on the market. This price structure has been further aggravated by the action taken by Peru in glutting the fish meal market, a by-product which helped maintain

the groundfish price for Canadian fishermen. As a matter of record, production of fish meal in Peru last year amounted to a figure between 300,000 and 400,000 tons. While this has had an effect on our east coast fishermen I know from the comments made by hon. members from British Columbia that it completely crippled the herring and whaling industries on Canada's west coast.
However, despite these setbacks the fishing industry can still look to the future with optimism. Canada has the sea at her front door on both coasts capable of supplying large quantities of highly edible protein seafood. We have, for instance, our great lobster fishery which though late in starting last year was generally productive throughout the summer and fall. Although there were some losses in equipment the season was considered the most successful for many years.
In the maritimes and Quebec our total fisheries products were valued at approximately $33 million with lobsters making up over $14 million of the total. I have already mentioned our scallop industry and its great potential in the maritimes. At the present time efforts are being made to include scallops on the menus for the personnel of our armed forces and if approved by the joint services food and nutrition committee this should add greatly to our marketing of this delectable sea food. I checked with the Department of National Defence and ascertained that over a recent 12-month period according to the information provided by the armed forces there has been procured for issue to units in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island a total of 85,788 pounds of fresh frozen halibut, haddock, sole and scallops as compared with 53,714 pounds of fresh frozen salmon. Some 400 pounds of scallops were purchased at the special request of the United States air force personnel in the area.
I submit to the committee that if scallops are good enough for the United States services they are good enough for our Canadian armed forces personnel. The joint services food and nutritional committee has been requested to add scallops to food lists provided that the price is not excessive in relation to other similar commodities. I would hope they will be found acceptable and that this will provide a new outlet for our scallops.
Our oyster beds have been restocked and are improving and there is still a good market in the United States for our swordfish, a branch of the fishing industry that has grown to great proportions in the last ten years and annually provides increased income for our east coast fishermen. I might add that swordfishing is practically a by-product of the department's efforts to improve the lot of the

inhore fishermen by subsidizing long-liners. It is a very profitable industry for long-liners during the months of June, July, August and part of September when ground fishing is not too profitable. These long-liners are equipped with a stand containing a pulpit that protrudes some 20 feet in front of the boat. A high mast and steering equipment are arranged. These long-liners geared for swordfishing range the coast from the banks of Maine to Sable island and off the coast of Cape Breton. The catch is almost entirely sold in the United States markets and it adds greatly to the earnings of our east coast fishermen.
Marketing problems still must be resolved but the work carried out by the department's home economists throughout Canada in preparing recipes and in promoting the use of fish with women's groups, church groups, hotel and restaurant associations and institutes has helped considerably to make Canadians aware of the value of fish.
The second phase that has been helpful is the amount of direct advertising carried out in connection with the consumer work of the home economists. The advertisements placed in daily and weekly newspapers and in mass circulation magazines plus the work of the consumer branch has been most helpful in increasing the consumption of fish in Canada. However, in my opinion most Canadians seem to be pretty well fed and our job is to replace other food with fish. Here I must throw out a word of caution to the Department of Agriculture and point out the desirability of putting an end to artificial price supports which cause over-production in the competitive food field. For example, recent offerings of canned pork on the domestic market at less than cost have the effect of encouraging consumers to buy the subsidized product while the fishing industry must sell its products on the basis of quality and nutritional value.
Although the problems I have mentioned require continuous study by the Department of Fisheries and the industry I believe that the present diversification of our fishing industry plus the vast markets opened up by new methods of transportation and refrigeration offer greater opportunity than ever before to Canada's fishermen.

I do not think there was anything more important said in the debate-and I must say this is almost a love feast, as the estimates of the Department of Fisheries nearly always are-than what was said by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg about fishing vessels. I am not going to recommend to the government any particular method; I am going to draw to the minister's attention-I do not need to draw it to his attention but I am going to do it so that it will be on the record-a resolution which was passed unanimously at the last meeting of the fisheries council of Canada in Vancouver in May on the importation of fishing vessels, which reads:
Whereas some processors of fish are suffering severely from lack of suitable fishing vessels; and
Whereas the federal government restricts the acquisition of the desired craft in the foreign markets through:
(a)	The necessity of having to secure permission from the Department of Transport to import a vessel-a restriction which we do not believe exists in the case of instruments of production in any other Canadian primary industry;
(b)	Heavy duties levied on vessels up to 100 feet in length when imported from most favoured nation countries; and
Whereas experience has shown that larger vessels are going to play a more important part in production in future years;
Therefore be it resolved that the fisheries council of Canada request the federal government to remove these hindrances to the adequate building up of the Canadian fishing fleet.
I do not think these are the only hindrances. I think the hon. member and some other hon. members who have spoken have put their fingers on other things.

In this parliament we have established a new agricultural bank to provide credit. It is true it is a successor to the old farm loan board, but it has a wider scope and at least it is supposed to do the job much better than the farm loan board did. In the fisheries improvement loans legislation we have the equivalent of the farm improvement loans legislation but we have nothing to compare with the agricultural development bank. I think we should have a fisheries development bank. I do not say it should be set up as a separate institution. Perhaps we should make it a branch of the agricultural development bank, because I do not want to see a whole lot more money spent in overhead; but there is no more reason why the people of Canada should subscribe the capital for loans to farmers than there is that they should subscribe it for fishermen. Indeed, both these primary industries, and the fishery even more than many branches of agriculture, have to compete on world markets at world prices, as hon. members have pointed out, largely without any kind of support, and the fishermen have to buy everything they buy in a largely protected market.
As the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg pointed out, this does create a real disability because the fisherman cannot raise his prices. He cannot raise his prices because the price is the price in the world, and if we were to try to raise our prices for our salt fish or our fresh frozen fish, or anything else we produce, somebody else is willing to sell it and we lose the market. We can make the industry as efficient as possible, and that is very important, but we also are faced in almost every branch of the fisheries in the world today, and this is particularly true of salt fish, with subsidies of one form and another to every one of our competitors in the world.
For example, the hon. member referred to the most recent legislation in the United States having to do with assistance in building vessels. I do think that our whole bounty program needs to be looked at again and looked at again in the light of world conditions and of the balance between the fishing industry and other industries. To my way of thinking the whole business of bounties, the whole business of loans of all kinds on fishing craft, small craft as well as larger craft, needs to be looked at.
The other thing is that at the end of the war this country removed all the taxes on agricultural implements so that agricultural implements could be bought at world prices. Surely if we can do that for the agricultural

industry we should do it for the fishing industry, and get rid of all the red tape that has existed in the acquisition of vessels in the past.
I do urge the government to take a bold step. The minister may perhaps have to knock the Minister of Transport on the head a few times, but he ought to have help from the Minister of National Revenue who ought to know something about this and who, as a matter of fact, collects some of those imposts that ought not to be there at all. I do hope that something quite serious will be done in this field.
There is another field-and here I speak more of Newfoundland perhaps than of any other part of Canada-in which something could be done. What is very desperately needed in Newfoundland, and what is going to be very hard to get except with the spread of rural electrification, and that is taking place, is some imaginative assistance in the establishment of local cold storage facilities which would not be used merely for the storage of fish but could also be used for the storage of vegetables and other foodstuffs sort of on a community basis, perhaps on a rather smaller scale than under the Cold Storage Act for agriculture. There is no doubt whatever that one thing that could be done that would vastly improve the standard of living in those fishing settlements would be to establish facilities for preserving food, for refrigeration, so that all food except fish itself would not be so costly and so that fish itself could be preserved in the community in a way which would make it palatable for the greater part of the year. I believe that an immensely greater amount of fish could be consumed in the fishing areas of Canada and all through the maritime provinces. I had occasion to visit Nova Scotia not so long ago -I do not recall this with any particular satisfaction although I had a very good time -and it was remarked to me there what we know to be true in Newfoundland and what I have found to be true in nearly all those fishing settlements, that if you want to go out to buy a fish to eat it is often a major operation. There really does need to be a lot more done than is being done now to get the people right around the places where the fish are caught to enjoy what is as good food as any food produced in this country.
In that context I should also like to say that I was very pleased to hear the minister say that the department had produced a new cook book, that the first edition was already sold out and that he is producing a second edition. But in order to create a real interest right here near at home I suggest that the minister send a complimentary copy to every

member of the house when the second run comes out with a little note that we take them to our wives with his compliments, or those of us who have not got wives, like the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, could perhaps find someone that they might attract in this way. It might be a lure.
I think one of the big problems in getting the consumption of fish in this country up to the level it has reached in almost every other country is that most people do not know how to cook fish and how to make it attractive. It is something that has to be learned like everything else. I shall never forget the story, which I am sure was not true, about those charitable Nova Scotians who during the depths of the depression in the thirties sent a carload of salt codfish to Saskatchewan to help the farmers who, as a result of a combination of all the dreadful circumstances there were then, were having a very thin time indeed. Some time afterward the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix published a recipe for cooking this codfish and this was the recipe: Nail the codfish to a board, boil for three hours, throw away the codfish and eat the board.
That story does no credit to Saskatchewan because there is nothing better than salt codfish as a food if you know how to treat it. But that is not the way to treat it and it should never be treated that way. That is why I say it is most important to carry on this work of promotion. The fishing industry, as all of us know, is in many ways a marginal industry. It is marginal because it is carried on on the coasts. It is marginal because on the whole the staple product of the fishery is, unfortunately, sold in low price markets. It is marginal because the mark-up is small. It is marginal because in the main the product is not processed by great combines in the way that canned pork and some other things are. Therefore, in order to be put on an equal level with some of our other industries it does need perhaps a little more careful assistance, not as a permanent crutch but in order to stimulate the market because, as the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has said and as we who represent fishing communities all desire, we want the industry to be strong and self-supporting.
We know from all the evidence around us that in the next few years we are going to have, because of the very rapid growth in our population, a large number of young people coming on the labour market every year, and we need to conserve and stimulate and build up in every way possible in order to employ our people productively. The last thing we want to see is a decline in this the oldest historic industry of our country. But 79951-0-351

The idea that one can arbitrarily cut these allowances without having reference to the true facts, without making any accurate survey in the north, or without having any regard to the hidden factors which come to bear on the increased cost of living in the north is completely unacceptable. It costs more to transport goods into the north; it costs more to transport goods out of the north. If we are to establish any industry up there, including a commercial fishing industry, those costs must be pared to just as low a point as they possibly can be pared. I think if the limitations were enforced you may as well not consider the establishment of a fishing industry there at all because transportation costs would be such as would place the cost of the product produced there completely out of the selling markets of southern Canada.
In my view the maximum permissible loadings and their effect on the problem of transportation are most important in developing a primary industry there. We must sell the products that we produce in the Yukon at competitive world prices despite the inherent cost of their production. In the north of Canada our highways are the counterpart of the railroads which serve industry in the most densely populated areas. We must regard them with equal importance to our economy. I would be most grateful for anything the minister could do to remove these suffocating and needless regulations.
The question of isolated post allowances could be cured, I am sure posthaste, if the true facts were known to those who have the authority of making these recommendations to treasury board, and I refer again to the interdepartmental committee on isolated post

regulations. If these people would make an accurate survey of the true cost of living there instead of working on supposition, guesswork and arbitrary estimations, they would find that the reductions which have been imposed are completely unjustified.
