It is my hope that any efforts made by the minister to alleviate these two situations will bring about a favourable consideration of the problems I have mentioned with regard to the establishment of a commercial fishing industry in the north, and I hope that these proposals will bear fruit.

Mr. Chairman, may I make a comment or two on this particular item. Perhaps first of all I may be allowed to express my feelings with regard to one of the officials of the department who will shortly be retiring, namely Mr. Whitmore who is the director of fisheries in the Pacific area. Mr. Whitmore has been in the department for some 40 years now or a bit longer, having held various positions, and as an indication of the degree of respect and admiration which exists for him throughout the entire fishing industry perhaps I should make this slight reference to the words of praise and commendation which have been made of Mr. Whitmore by various organizations interested in the fishing industry on the west coast.
The fisheries association of British Columbia honoured Mr. Whitmore not too long ago, as did the united fishermen and allied workers union and the native brotherhood of British Columbia; and also more recently the department itself made a presentation to Mr. Whitmore for his long years of dedicated service. The fisheries association and the united fishermen's union I would say in normal events disagree with each other, because one represents the industry and one is a union; but this is indicative of the respect that Mr. Whitmore has generated over the years so far as his attitude and his administration of fisheries on the coast is concerned. I would hope that even after his retirement he will remain in a position where the department will feel free to call upon him for any advice, and that he will remain a member of the international salmon fisheries commission so that his years of experience will not be lost entirely to the department and to the agencies and commissions which function within the department.
I would also like to make a brief comment with respect to the Fraser river and the salmon industry on the coast. The Fraser
Supply-Fisheries
river, of course, is the most important salmon river which exists either in British Columbia or anywhere in the world and its value to the economy of the province is well known by everyone in British Columbia and to the departmental officials. Some thought has been expressed, mostly by those people in our economy who are more concerned with hydroelectric power than they are with the fishing industry and the products derived therefrom, about attempts to build hydroelectric and flood control dams on the Fraser river. Some of the dams which have beeen proposed range up to 700 or 800 feet in height, and I think it almost goes without saying that even although a tremendous amount of research work has been undertaken in recent years in an attempt to overcome the bad effect of dams on fish and to make sure the fish maintain themselves and that the river is not destroyed, this attempt is only effective to a slight degree. If dams like the Moran dam, which stands some 700 feet, were built it would completely destroy the Fraser river as a fish river. The minister need look no further than the Columbia river, which runs partly in Canada and partly in the United States, where hydroelectric storage dams have been built. Regardless of the $150 million odd which has been spent in the United States, I understand, in an attempt to retain the Columbia as a fish river, the efforts have been practically ineffectual so far as the fish are concerned.
One of the very fine things in this regard for the fisheries interests are the discussions which are presently taking place between the Canadian government, the British Columbia government, and the United States so far as further development for hydroelectric purposes on the Columbia river are concerned. This, coupled with the possibility of a hydroelectric development further north on the Peace river, has already gone a great deal of the way toward diminishing the demands and the insistance of the hydroelectric interests to build dams on the Fraser river. I hope that by the time nuclear energy becomes economically competitive or even less costly than hydro development, by the time we reach that age of nuclear power we shall have developed sufficient non-fish rivers for hydroelectric purposes and that we will no longer-need to worry about the Fraser river being; ruined as a fish river. That is my hope and I am sure it is the hope of the Department of Fisheries. This needs re-emphasis and reinforcement from time to time by the people interested. The Fraser river and other fish rivers on the coast should be protected at all possible cost and the energies of the electric power people should be directed toward other

Supply-Fisheries
means of producing electrical energy instead of ruining these great rivers and the contribution they make toward our economy.
This question of the Fraser river and multiple use of it was studied and is still being studied by an agency established by joint participation of the federal and provincial governments, upon which agency the Department of Fisheries have representation. I refer here to the Fraser river board. While this board is established under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources I think it still has some bearing on this particular department because the river with which it deals is a fish river and the interests of the department are involved one way or the other.
This may be the time to communicate to the minister, as has been done on other occasions, the need for him to press as hard as he can with his colleagues, especially the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, for some sort of flood control activity on the Fraser river. I refer to control that would not have a deleterious effect on the fishing industry on that river.
I have in my hand a report dealing with multiple uses of the Fraser river and the question of flood control by building a series of dams in the upper reaches of the Fraser and employing other methods of control in the lower reaches. I believe our efforts should be bent toward developing a diking system in the lower reaches of the Fraser rather than concentrating on building storage dams in the upper reaches where they will interfere with the spawning activities of the fish.
To illustrate the value of diking as opposed to building storage dams I will refer to the report. This approaches the question from the point of view of economy without reference to the fishery aspect. The report indicates that the building up of the present dikes in the lower reaches of the Fraser to the point needed to meet the flood level of 1894 which is the highest point of which they have knowledge would cost $17 million plus annual operating costs as compared with $520 million for the building of reservoirs and star storage dams. We are not dealing with the question of flood control specifically so I will not violate the rules by pursuing this subject.
I turn now to the conflict of interest that exists between the fisheries and forests. From time to time in the forests of Canada we have insect infestations. The forestry people wanting to ensure the continued growth of forests have embarked on programs of spraying the trees with insecticide the use of which results in killing not only the insects but fish

because of the toxic effect of the insecticide. It washes down the hillsides with the soil and is carried into the streams containing fish. This problem has occupied the attention of the Department of Fisheries which has studied the question and attempted to find an innocuous insecticide that would not be harmful to fish. I am not aware that they have met with success in their research but I hope their efforts will continue.
There is a conflict of interest here. One must either choose between seeing damage to forests or damage to the fisheries or one must seek to strike a balance. Both the federal and provincial forestry people have sought to achieve a balance. I urge that there be a continuing intensive research program in this field.
In the supplementary estimates there is an item in the amount of $150,000 for the destruction of dogfish and other predators. This is the third year to my knowledge that there has been an item for this purpose. I appreciate that in the last couple of years many difficulties have been encountered in effectively implementing the program. I will not deal with the problem other than to say it has not been as successful as it might have been. The fishing industry on the west coast has been critical in several respects of the approach to the problem adopted by the department. I appreciate that it is difficult for the departmental officials to ask the treasury board for approval for further monetary provision in this field when all the moneys allotted have not been expended but I earnestly hope they will persevere in their efforts in years to come.
The attitude of the treasury board would be something like this. You were here two or three years ago and we gave you $250,000. You spent hardly any of it. Last year we gave you another $200,000 and you did not use that. Now you want some more money. How long is this going to continue? The treasury board will have to have results for any money allocated, and this is the thing we should look for if we do not embark on an effective dogfish killing program so that these predators are eliminated to the greatest possible extent.
I should like to make reference to another matter which involves the Department of Agriculture. I refer to the subsidies paid under the Cold Storage Act. As hon. members well know this is under the Department of Agriculture. Fish products cold storage warehouses are built from time to time and a subsidy is payable on those fish products warehouses by and through the Department of Agriculture. Two or three years ago the Department of Agriculture saw fit to place some limitations upon the amount of subsidy

paid. The reason for doing that was that there was, as it were, a glut of cold storage warehouses in Canada and to continue to pay one-third of the cost as a subsidy without limitation on the total amount merely meant that the federal government would be paying money in the form of subsidies to build more and more cold storage warehouses at a time when there were too many of them already in existence. The arguments were that the bulk of cold storage warehouses in Canada are for agricultural products. This tends to work out to the advantage of the Department of Agriculture and the agricultural industry but it places the fishing industry at a disadvantage because it has its activities curtailed by the activities in the agricultural field.
We have asked a number of times for the transfer of jurisdiction so that subsidies payable for fish cold storage warehouses would be used to build cold storage warehouses under the jurisdiction of the Department of Fisheries. We feel that the Department of Fisheries are able to do a much better and a more efficient job in the building of those warehouses and in the paying of the subsidies than the Department of Agriculture. As I say, this has been dealt with a number of times in the past. We have asked questions of the Minister of Agriculture and of the Minister of Fisheries. The answers which we have received on each occasion in the past have been, "Well, we will consult about this". If I am not mistaken, I think the Minister of Fisheries said in the marine and fisheries committee when the estimates of the department were being considered that the suggestion I had made at that time sounded like a sensible one and he would give it sympathetic and earnest or some other type of consideration; that he would have a talk with his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, about it, to see if some arrangement could be worked out. I should like to have an indication from the minister of the results of those discussions. What plan, if any, has been worked out to bring this matter under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries in so far as fish products are concerned so that full and proper consideration can be given to any application for a subsidy for the erection of a fish products cold storage warehouse so that the fisheries industry will not be placed at a disadvantage because of the activities in the agricultural products field? This, I submit, is the situation at the moment.
I have one other point, and this again I think is something which in reality could more properly be dealt with by the Department of External Affairs. Nevertheless, it does concern the fishing industry and the Department of Fisheries because our offshore
Supply-Fisheries
fishing rights are involved in the territorial limits of the country extending out into the ocean.
The so-called proposal for a 12-mile limit has been discussed at international conferences. It was discussed at the recent one, just a month or so ago; it was discussed at the United Nations general assembly and prior to that time at another conference on the law of the sea. There were suggestions from different countries as to what those territorial limits should be. So far we have come to no conclusion on them.
The latest proposal of Canada for a six and six arrangement was defeated, I understand, by one third of a vote or something like that, but it was just defeated and that was all. This would make one wonder whether there is any great sense in going further and further into international conferences on this particular question because I think Canada, in its desire to reach agreement on the question of our territorial limits, did depart from our original thought that there should be a 12-mile limit when it suggested six and six. I think Canada went a bit too far in that regard in an attempt to reach an agreement. I do not think it would be wise for us to go any further in that direction. Perhaps the most appropriate thing to do, so far as our general limits are concerned, is to take unilateral action and declare as Iceland has declared and as others are considering now, that our territorial limits for all purposes are 12 miles, and that is that.
This would overcome, of course, what I consider to be an extremely ridiculous situation on the east coast which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and other members from the Atlantic provinces will have more intimate personal knowledge of than I. I refer to difficulties which arise from having two sorts of limits, a three-mile limit and a 12-mile limit. This affects our fishermen. Some of them have to go out beyond our 12-mile limit in order to fish while foreign fishermen can come inside the 12-mile limit and fish. By unilateral action on our part, which I think is the only course necessary, we would overcome this problem without too much difficulty. Of course, in so doing we might create other difficulties such as impairing our relations with the United States. This is primarily why Canada has been weak-kneed and weak-hearted in this particular field. But none the less I think it is about time we did realize that it may be necessary to incur strained relations once in a while in order to reach that goal which is just and fair.

In this regard, I think, as I said, this is primarily an external affairs matter. Nevertheless, the fishery interests are involved and I think, taking everything into consideration, Canada should now say that our territorial waters extend to 12 miles beyond our shores. After all, if a small nation like Iceland, apparently reflecting a great deal of the courage of that government, courage which this government does not appear to have, can take such action, then surely Canada in the same light can take the same action to protect our interests.

First, I want to congratulate the minister on the steps his department has taken in the field of the conservation of the fisheries on the Pacific coast. In his opening remarks this morning he spoke of a project on Robertson creek near Great Central lake on Vancouver island. I think he might well have enlarged on that a bit because it appears to be a credit to the department and so far it has been very successful.
I should like to call to the minister's attention and ask him to comment later on the necessity for a somewhat similar and perhaps larger conservation project on the Big Quali-cum river near Qualicum Beach, also on the island. I should also like to call his attention to the need for action on the Puntledge river near Courtenay. This river was adversely affected from the fish spawning point of view a few years ago by the enlargement of a hydro power project by the British Columbia power commission which at the time did not appear to give much regard to their responsibility with respect to fish conservation. In the same area there is need for further development on the Tsolum river which has been a very heavy spawning stream in years gone by, particularly for pinks. During the summer months and the early fall when the pinks go up the river there is often very low water and they cannot get up the river to spawn with the result that sometimes a pretty large crop is destroyed. I believe that the fisheries department is considering a storage dam at Wolf lake at the head of the river and I would ask that construction of the dam be expedited as quickly as possible.
There is another question I have already brought to the attention of the minister by letter and I should like to mention it again. I refer to the problem of the blackfish or killer whales interfering with the salmon fishing, especially in the gulf of Georgia and the inside waters along the east coast of Vancouver island. I know this is a difficult problem. Some interests that are concerned about it have suggested setting up machine gun posts but that would probably result in killing half the fishermen on the coast as

well as visitors and sports fishermen. It is a very difficult problem. So far as I know, the department has no real answer to it yet but I hope they will keep working on it and perhaps come up with an answer.
We had quite a little excitement in the coastal area a few months ago when there was a suggestion that a licensing system would be set up for sports fishermen. I have talked to a good many fishermen and a number of resort operators along the coast and they are of the opinion that perhaps this is necessary in order that the department can plan proper conservation programs and keep some control over the catch of fish by sportsmen or at least know what they are catching. In general the thought is, and I also feel this way about the matter, that if such a licence is required the charge should be very nominal. The feeling is that these licences may be required in order to keep a record of fishing and keep control of sport fishing in the same way that provincial forest fire permits are issued. Those permits are issued free but in this case perhaps the charge might be sufficient to cover the cost of administration of the licensing system.
The preceding speaker, the hon. member for Skeena, spoke about the Fraser river board and opposed the adoption of system A as they term it in their report. I think he left, I trust unintentionally, a wrong impression in his comparison of costs. I do not have the exact figures with me but the figure he quoted of some $500 million, if that figure is correct, also included the cost of a considerable hydro power installation on the Clearwater river above any spawning areas. No spawning grounds would be affected by this development, so I wanted to correct any wrong impression that might have been left in that respect.
In the recently presented second report of the committee on mines, forests and waters, the committee after careful study of the Fraser river board report and after hearing from the representatives of the fisheries department on the board made the following recommendation:
Your committee heard evidence from the two federal members of the Fraser river board concerning what is referred to in the board's preliminary report dated June, 1958, as system A. Since this proposed system A appears to offer the best possible chance of fulfilling the following objectives, (1) to provide flood control: (2) to be an integral part of a major power system; (3) to be compatible with fisheries; and (4) to be economically self-supporting through power production, your committee recommends that the further studies to establish the physical feasibility of projects in system A and the required additional biological studies relating to fisheries interests be actively pursued. This is in order that a final conclusion as to the merits of system A may be reached at the earliest possible date.

I think that is the proper way to approach the problem. I do not think we should come to any conclusions without proper evidence to support those conclusions.
I should also like to say a few words about the pending retirement of one of the senior officials of the fisheries department to whom the hon. member for Skeena also paid a compliment. We on the British Columbia coast have known Mr. Whitmore for many years. I believe he has served almost 45 years with the department and he certainly has been a credit to the department. We all hope that his successor will meet with the same support and be held in the same high esteem that Mr. Whitmore was.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw a few matters to the attention of the minister. First of all, I should like to take some exception to what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said with regard to the proposed licences for sport fishing in salt water. I feel that they accomplish no good purpose whatsoever. The amount of fish taken in salt water by sports fishermen is infinitesimal when compared with commercial catches. Grilse is the only fish of which any substantial number is caught and the department has a fair idea of what the take is at the present time. I cannot see sports fishermen filling out forms and sending them to the department. I do not know what the department can accomplish except to bring about more bureaucracy, and I am opposed to any such form of licensing with regard to sport fishing on the Pacific coast. So far as I have been able to ascertain, and I have inquired, there is no such licensing on the east coast, and I do not think it is necessary.

Would the hon. member allow me to ask a question? On what does he base his statement that the sport catch is infinitesimal? Nobody can possibly make a statement like that if they have examined the statistics.

Infinitesimal, I said, as compared with the commercial catch. Certainly there is a fairly large number of fish, but I do not think that it is of the order of importance that it is made out to be.
However, that is not really what I wanted to talk about. I do want to talk about the pollution of streams and the fact that I believe the Fisheries Act needs to be overhauled and more teeth put in it to give the minister and his officials more authority to do something in regard to the control of pollution of streams. I believe the fisheries department is doing an excellent job on the west coast, and undoubtedly in other areas in which they operate. I believe the
Supply-Fisheries
staff is able and conscientious but is perhaps limited by the fact the budget is not large enough or by the lack of trained personnel.
I believe, however, there needs to be a change in the legislation in order to put more teeth in the act. I have made a few notes in this connection and I find that under section 33 of the Fisheries Act the minister is given wide powers to control and prevent the pollution of fishing waters. This control extends to ships which shall not throw overboard ballast, coal ashes or other prejudicial or deleterious substances in any river, harbour or roadstead or in any water where fishing is carried on. It extends to plants which may not discharge industrial waste which may be harmful to fish and it extends to lumbering, land clearing or any such activities in the way of preventing such activities from putting any slash, stumps or debris into water frequented by fish or into water which may flow into a place frequented by fish. A salmon stream can be ruined by a log jam, a river made poisonous to fish from industrial waste and city discharged sewage.
The penalties for infractions of section 33 bear no relationship to the harm that can be done by an infraction. The first offence carries a penalty of $20 and costs; the second offence not less than $40 and costs and not more than $80 and costs, and in addition a further penalty of not less than $10 and not more than $20 for every day during which such offence is continued. The third, or any subsequent offence, carries a penalty of not less than $100 and costs and also in addition a further penalty not exceeding $20 for every day during which such offence is continued.
These penalties are extremely inadequate to be a proper deterrent. Ignoring the fines which are quite modest, the daily penalty of $20 for continuous infraction of the law is something any industrial plant of any size would find quite easy to pay and indeed might prefer to pay rather than undergo the expense of diverting or treating their waste liquids so as to comply with the law. This penalty of $20 a day is, in fact, the maximum penalty which can be assessed against any farmer who does not maintain an approved fish grating at the intake of an irrigation ditch drawing water from a fish producing stream. The fish grating guards against the occasional fish being destroyed, but the waste from an industrial plant can poison a whole stream.
I suggest that the minister should review these penalties and adjust them upward to the point where they will prove a real deterrent. Perhaps this could be done by bringing the Fisheries Act into parliament for amendment, if necessary, or through the regulations. Perhaps it might be better to add proper

Supply-Fisheries
fisheries pollution control regulations which could be amended by the minister himself on his own responsibility.
Second, there is the matter of pollution from ships either throwing ballast overboard, throwing garbage overboard or pumping bilges while actually in a river or within a harbour. The various harbour commissioners must guard against this, but the department has a responsibility as well. Finally, there is the effect on fish bearing streams of the discharge of sewage into them. It is well recognized, however, that this type of pollution is not as dangerous as industrial waste because of the way that industrial waste destroys the oxygen content in the water. Nevertheless, the pollution of streams from the discharge of sewage is an important factor and it is becoming an important factor on the Fraser river which, as the hon. member for Skeena has pointed out, is perhaps the greatest remaining salmon fishing stream in the world since the Columbia was destroyed as a salmon river. It is imperative that the fisheries department have authority and power to guard against the break-down of our fisheries or the diminution of our streams.
The submission to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by the fisheries association of British Columbia pointed out that commercial fishing is the fourth largest primary industry of the province, preceded only by forestry, agriculture and mining. They pointed out also that this important industry provides employment for some 18,000 persons and they estimated that another 75,000 persons were indirectly dependent upon the industry for employment. The salmon fishery of British Columbia, according to this submission, could be at least doubled within the next 25 years. We do have an intimation, highlighted by the unions I believe, that there is too much gear in the water. There is one side of the equation. You can either have too much gear or too few fish. You can build up the fish so as to support the gear and the number of fishermen who are engaged in that activity. I suggest that the experience of the fisheries department at Jones Creek and Horsefly and other places that were mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has proved the admirable work the department has done. It is simply too bad that money cannot be provided to accelerate this program because there must be at least 20 or 30 other streams up and down the coast of British Columbia which could be prepared with artificial spawning beds, which could be stocked with pinks and thus build up the runs of fish which are not as valuable as sockeye. However, a very valuable fishery could be built up to fill in the offrun years.

Again this report refers to the experiment at Jones Creek and it is stated that it has been proved now that (a) an artificial gravel bed can be built which will be as efficient or more so than the natural stream bed for the production of pink salmon fry and (b) pink salmon can be transplanted to a new area to provide runs of salmon in off years. Considering that the salmon fishery, not in the best years but in average years, is worth about $50 million; considering that by proper conservation methods the Adams river run was built up in 1958 to a run of 12 million fish when back 20 or 30 years ago it was down to a run of some 17,000 cases; considering that conservation measures can build up this resource and can provide a continuing source of God given wealth to this country and employment to the people of this country, I say that the fisheries department is perhaps one of the most important departments in the whole government. I sincerely trust that the minister will be able to secure the funds and the staff which will alow an acceleration in this program which, undoubtedly, his officials have ahead of them for the next 10 or 15 years.
In so far as the problem of dogfish is concerned, there is not much sense in adding to what has been said. However, I believe that if the subsidy is not used up I think it would be well for the government to take the initiative. Perhaps one of the reasons-this may be just an excuse that has been given to me- for the subsidy not being used up is the fact it has not been announced early enough so that the fishermen can fish for dogfish at a time when these predators congregate at the mouths of rivers when they are following runs of small herring and so on and where the fishermen could catch large numbers of them. I think the program for the control of dogfish should be announced early in the year. I believe there should be a conference between the department, the fishing companies and the fishermen and that, when agreement has been reached, the program should be set out well ahead of time so that if there is any delay in going after these predators, it can be laid right at the door of the fishermen.
I should like to make one last point and it is nothing that is under the jurisdiction of the minister. However, we will never have really effective fisheries on the west coast until labour and management learn to get together. In this particular instance the union it seems to me, is always spoiling for a fight with management and always looking for opportunities to create disturbances. As I say, this is one area in which the minister

certainly has no jurisdiction. I wish he had jurisdiction. However, these are troubles that will pass away.
My point is that we should build up our fisheries by proper scientific methods, by the methods which are being used by the department now, and should build them up as fast as possible because this is an area in which every dollar spent will return scores of dollars to the people of Canada and also as revenue to the government.

of our nation as a whole, producing and contributing in every way, I think should have special consideration. I have special concern for the fishermen and the industry in Labrador.
On the question of artificial bait lures, I may say that these are being used on an experimental and trial basis and have been available for a number of years. The research board has also done a considerable amount of research with regard to fish attractants and repellants from the point of view of possible bait usage and for the guidance of fish in their migration and other possible applications.
Several hon. members spoke of the matter of the equipment of ships and of a program which will allow the fishing industry to be modernized. This is a matter that is now being studied by an interdepartmental committee on an official level, and which I hope will be reporting to the government before long. I also hope that they will be able to come up with something really constructive that will help the fishing industry and also the shipbuilding industry at the same time. But as hon. members know it is a very knotty problem indeed.
Many interesting suggestions were made as to increasing the market for fish in Canada, and one suggestion was about the expanding market for salted cod in Toronto and various other areas. I might say that the maritime salted cod producers have been exploiting this market for quite some time and are shipping considerable quantities of salted fish to Toronto to cater to this particular market.
The hon. member for Yukon spoke of the need for additional staff in that area. I wish to report that an addition to the staff will take place very shortly in the area. We could still use more staff, and if we can arrange it perhaps in the future permission will be given for additional staff there. The importance of developing the industry in this area is well known and the hon. member's suggestions will be taken into consideration and given further study.
The hon. member for Skeena kindly made reference to Mr. Whitmore's retirement, as did the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I appreciate the recognition they have given him in this regard and I must say that he is a very fine example of the excellent type of officials and scientists who are serving this department and who have served it with dedication over the years. I am delighted to see this recognition being made here on the floor of the house.
The hon. member for Skeena also mentioned the conflict in some cases between forests

and fish and the need for spraying budworms in the forests to wipe out if possible these epidemics. I might say there is really no conflict because if the forests were destroyed there would be no fish in any case. We have been doing research in this regard and we are now hopeful that a spray has been devised of a concentration which will do the minimum damage to fish and yet be effective as far as budworms and other insects are concerned.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni wanted to know about the projects he referred to on Vancouver island. I might say that as far as Puntledge river is concerned negotiations are in progress with the British Columbia power commission. The department has proposed certain fishways and other fish protective measures, and these have been referred to the British Columbia energy board. My understanding is that the board has not reported on the problem yet. The Big Quali-cum project is a comprehensive water control program which should increase very considerably the capacity of that watershed to produce salmon, and good progress is being made on it. The Tsolum river one is in the suggestion stage and proposals have been made that this would be a useful project, but up to this time it has not been evaluated. As far as sports fishing licences are concerned, I think hon. members can rest at ease for the present because no action has been taken to introduce licensing for salt water sports fishermen.
I shall be glad to answer other questions as we go along. I see that it is not quite six o'clock yet so perhaps it might be possible to get the first item passed.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
know whether any hon. member of any other party wants to speak on this item, but I think I could say for our part that we would not have any objection to the item going through as long as it were understood that the hon. member for Gloucester who is our spokesman on this subject and who expected to be here but just is not here would be given reasonable latitude on some other item.

Just before the item carries I would like to draw to the attention of the minister the activities taking place under the Cold Storage Act, and perhaps the minister could indicate if there have been any results to the discussions he has had with his colleague the Minister of Agriculture in this regard.

Mr. Chairman,
there have been discussions between the departments in order to judge the practicability of the suggestions which were advanced by the hon. member for Skeena and others last year before the committee. It has not been

found that there is any practical way of dividing the operation into two or to put it under two administrations. In any case, however, we are still open to suggestions. I think the only way it could be done practically would be to duplicate the Cold Storage Act as far as the Department of Fisheries is concerned.

I do not want to delay this unnecessarily but may I pose this problem. The Department of Agriculture deals primarily with agricultural products and the subsidies paid under that department, and under that department the interests of the fisheries is not given full consideration. If the only solution is duplication so that the fisheries department will have an establishment to deal with this sort of thing, I submit we must do that. As I understand the explanation given to me, this has been dealt with by the fisheries department anyway. If an application is made for a subsidy for fish cold storage warehouses I understand that the fisheries department is fully consulted on the matter as to whether a subsidy will be paid or not.
That is true.

So you already have duplication except that you do not have duplication in paying the subsidy. That results in the fisheries interests being injured or restricted because of the predominance of agricultural problems in the Department of Agriculture which have resulted in the Department of Agriculture placing a $50,000 limit on subsidies.
I suggest the only solution appears to be one of duplication. Apparently the machinery already exists and perhaps it may require an act comparable to the Cold Storage Act but applying to fishery products. Perhaps if the minister could indicate now what some of the difficulties are which he has found in his discussions, then I would not be so adamant in my approach and perhaps the problem is not too difficult.

I would like to say that I think there might be exceptions, but generally speaking full weight has been given to the recommendation and the advice given to the department officials when grants were made under this act applying to fisheries. There is the question of the limitation, and I think this is the nub of the problem.

A different act or any division in responsibility would not make any difference unless this limitation were raised or eliminated.
I think that is the crux of the problem which the hon. member has in mind because it might under certain circumstances bear unfairly upon a particular project. I believe I have an idea of what the hon. gentleman has in mind. This is due to the limitation in the act itself rather than the method of administration.
It is due to an order in council which put a ceiling of $50,000 on the subsidy. It is not due to the limitation in the act at all.
That is correct. I should have said it is due to the regulations made under the act.
Is the minister agreeable to the suggestion I made?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Item agreed to.
Resolution adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the house leader if he could indicate the order in which estimates will be taken tomorrow and if there is anything definite he can say about Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the house will find it agreeable tomorrow to complete the estimates of the Department of Fisheries and then make a start on those of the Department of Justice. It is a question of the allocation of time. We will have available for discussion about 6J hours tomorrow after orders of the day are reached.
If another department was needed what would it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The third item would be completion of the estimates of the Department of Transport in case the house moves rapidly.
For Friday the first item of business would be the bill of rights. The question of hours of sitting on Friday has not yet been determined by the house.
It being five minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
